title: Ordo Virtutum
creator: Hildegard of Bingen
location: Probably first performed at Rupertsberg convent, near Bingen
description: Hildegard wrote the Ordo Virtutum (Play of the Virtues) around 1151, probably for the nuns of her new convent at Rupertsberg, and a short version of it closes her visionary book Scivias. It dramatises the struggle for a human soul, Anima, between sixteen Virtues and the Devil. Anima at first rejoices, then grows weary of the Virtues' discipline and is lured away by the Devil, before returning penitent and wounded to be welcomed back, while the Virtues bind the Devil. All the characters sing in Hildegard's soaring, wide-ranging chant except the Devil, who can only speak or shout, a striking image of evil as the absence of harmony. It is the oldest known morality play by several centuries and survives with its music in the Riesenkodex at Wiesbaden. Rediscovered in modern times, it has been staged and recorded many times since the 1980s.

title: Magnus liber organi
creator: Léonin
location: Notre-Dame Cathedral, Paris; survives in manuscripts now in Florence, Wolfenbüttel and Madrid
description: The Magnus liber organi, the Great Book of Organum, was the collection of polyphonic settings of chant for the main feasts of the church year used at Notre-Dame in Paris. The theorist known as Anonymous IV credited its first form to Léonin and its revision to Pérotin. It contained organa for two voices in which a sustained chant underpins a florid upper voice, along with sections in measured discant. The book itself does not survive; its contents are known from three large later manuscripts, the most important now in the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana in Florence, each preserving a different stage of revision. The book's rhythmic notation, based on patterns of long and short notes, was one of the first ways of writing rhythm precisely. Together these collections are the starting point of the history of composed polyphony in the West.

title: Viderunt omnes (organum quadruplum)
creator: Pérotin
location: Notre-Dame Cathedral, Paris (Christmas, probably from 1198)
description: Viderunt omnes is the gradual chant for Christmas Day, and Pérotin's setting for four voices is one of the grandest works of the Notre-Dame school. An edict of Bishop Odo of Sully in 1198 ordered organum in three or four parts for the Christmas season, and this setting is usually linked with it. The lowest voice sings the original chant in enormously long held notes, so that a single syllable may last a minute, while three upper voices weave rhythmic patterns above it in the long-short rhythmic modes, echoing and swapping phrases. The result is a radiant wall of sound suited to the vast new Gothic cathedral then under construction. Only the solo portions of the chant were set in polyphony; the choir sang the rest in plain chant. The work survives in several manuscripts of the Magnus liber and has become one of the most recorded pieces of medieval music.

title: Ma fin est mon commencement
creator: Guillaume de Machaut
location: Preserved in Machaut's collected manuscripts
description: The title of this rondeau, 'My end is my beginning', describes its construction. The top voice, sung backwards, gives the second voice, and the third voice reaches its midpoint and then repeats itself in reverse, so that the whole piece is a palindrome. Machaut's text explains the puzzle, which was meant as much to be solved by the eye as heard. Despite the ingenuity, the music works as a graceful courtly song in the rondeau form, with its refrain returning between verses. The motto was later embroidered by Mary, Queen of Scots, and T. S. Eliot inverted it in Four Quartets. The piece is a good example of the delight in intellectual design that runs through medieval music.

title: Messe de Nostre Dame
creator: Guillaume de Machaut
location: Probably Reims Cathedral
description: Machaut's Messe de Nostre Dame sets the six main sung sections of the Mass Ordinary, Kyrie, Gloria, Credo, Sanctus, Agnus Dei and the closing Ite missa est, for four voices. It was probably written in the 1360s for Reims Cathedral, where Machaut was a canon, and may have been sung at a Saturday mass of the Virgin for which he and his brother endowed prayers after their deaths. Earlier masses had been assembled from pieces by different composers; this is the first known complete cycle conceived by one author. The Gloria and Credo, with their long texts, move in mostly chordal style, while the other movements are isorhythmic, built on chant melodies laid out in repeating rhythmic patterns in the tenor. The harmony, with its open fifths and sharp dissonances, sounds austere and strange to modern ears. It is the best-known work of fourteenth-century music.

title: Nuper rosarum flores
creator: Guillaume Du Fay
location: Florence Cathedral, consecration, 25 March 1436
description: Pope Eugenius IV consecrated Florence Cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, on 25 March 1436, after Brunelleschi had completed his great dome, and Du Fay, then a singer in the papal chapel, wrote this motet for the ceremony. Its text speaks of roses given by the pope to the church. Two lower voices sing a chant melody, Terribilis est locus iste, in canon at the fifth, while two upper voices weave freer lines above. The work falls into four sections whose lengths are in the proportion 6:4:2:3, and a much-discussed theory proposed that these mirror the proportions of the cathedral or of Solomon's Temple; later scholars have questioned the link to the building. Either way, it is a superb example of music written for a specific moment of civic and religious splendour.

title: Ave Maria ... virgo serena
creator: Josquin des Prez
location: Printed in Petrucci's Motetti A, Venice, 1502
description: This motet, a prayer to the Virgin Mary, was probably written in the 1480s and appeared as the first piece in Petrucci's first book of motets in 1502. It opens with each voice entering in turn with the same phrase, from soprano down to bass, a technique called pervading imitation. Later sections alternate between pairs of voices in dialogue, full textures and a passage in triple time, following the stanzas of the poem, which greets five feasts of Mary's life. It ends with a short plea in chordal style, 'O Mother of God, remember me'. Its clarity, balance and sensitivity to text made it a classic, and it has been called the 'Mona Lisa' of Renaissance music. The dating once proposed as early as the 1470s remains debated.

title: Missa L'homme armé super voces musicales
creator: Josquin des Prez
location: First printed in Petrucci's Misse Josquin, Venice, 1502
description: The popular song L'homme armé (The armed man) served as the basis for more than forty Renaissance masses, and Josquin wrote two. In the Missa super voces musicales he places the tune in the tenor on a different step of the hexachord (ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la) in each successive movement, so that the melody climbs through the mass. Within this frame he includes mensuration canons, in which one melody is sung simultaneously at different speeds, most famously in the Agnus Dei. The work opened the first printed collection devoted entirely to one composer, Ottaviano Petrucci's Misse Josquin of 1502. It shows how a Renaissance composer could fuse intellectual design with fluent, euphonious music.

title: Missa Pange lingua
creator: Josquin des Prez
location: Printed posthumously, Nuremberg, 1539
description: The Missa Pange lingua is based on the plainchant hymn Pange lingua, sung at the feast of Corpus Christi, and is probably one of Josquin's last masses. Rather than placing the borrowed tune in long notes in the tenor, as older masses did, Josquin paraphrases it freely in all four voices, so that motifs from the hymn pass through the whole texture. The style is spare and transparent, with much writing for pairs of voices, and the Et incarnatus of the Credo moves into hushed chords. The mass circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1539. It is admired as an example of Josquin's late, concentrated style.

title: Missa Papae Marcelli
creator: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
location: Printed in Palestrina's Missarum liber secundus, Rome, 1567
description: The Pope Marcellus Mass is named after Marcellus II, who reigned for only three weeks in 1555 and reportedly urged that church music be sung with reverence and intelligible words. Palestrina's six-voice setting balances polyphonic richness with unusual clarity of text, especially in the long Gloria and Credo, where voices often declaim together. A story first told decades later, and elaborated in Hans Pfitzner's 1917 opera Palestrina, holds that the mass convinced the Council of Trent not to ban polyphony; historians regard this as a legend, though the Council did debate the intelligibility of sacred music. The work was printed in 1567 and became the classic model of Counter-Reformation polyphony, sung in the Sistine Chapel for centuries.

title: Spem in alium
creator: Thomas Tallis
location: Probably Arundel House or Nonsuch Palace, England; earliest source 1610s
description: Spem in alium (I have never put my hope in any other) is written for eight choirs of five voices each, forty separate parts. Its origins are uncertain; a later account suggests it was composed to rival an Italian work for forty voices, perhaps by Alessandro Striggio, who visited London in 1567. It may have been performed at Arundel House in London or at Nonsuch Palace. The music begins with a single voice, and the sound passes around the choirs, which would have stood in a ring, before all forty join in great climaxes, with dramatic pauses before the close. The oldest surviving source was copied for the investiture of Henry as Prince of Wales in 1610 with an English text. It is a landmark of the English Renaissance and has inspired modern works, including Janet Cardiff's sound installation The Forty Part Motet.

title: Lagrime di San Pietro
creator: Orlande de Lassus
location: Published in Munich, 1595
description: Lassus completed this cycle in May 1594, three weeks before his death, and dedicated it to Pope Clement VIII. It sets twenty stanzas from Luigi Tansillo's poem on Peter's remorse after denying Christ three times, followed by a Latin motet in which Christ speaks from the cross. The seven voices may symbolise the seven sorrows of the Virgin or the seven deadly sins, and the cycle moves systematically through the eight church modes. The music is grave, intensely expressive and harmonically searching, the work of a composer who had suffered from depression in his last years. It is regarded as the culmination of the spiritual madrigal.

title: Mass for Five Voices
creator: William Byrd
location: Printed privately in London without title page, c. 1595
description: Byrd published three masses, for four, three and five voices, between about 1592 and 1595, each a single slim set of part-books without a title page, which would have reduced the danger of owning them. They were intended for Catholic masses held in private houses, which were illegal in Elizabethan England, such as those at the Petre family's house in Essex. The five-voice mass is the most richly textured, using imitation and expressive word-setting with restraint suited to small groups of singers. Unlike Continental masses, which usually reworked existing music, Byrd's are freely composed. The Agnus Dei, with its plea for peace, is often heard as an expression of the plight of English Catholics. The masses were revived in the twentieth century and are sung in both Catholic and Anglican cathedrals.

title: Sonata pian' e forte
creator: Giovanni Gabrieli
location: Published in Sacrae symphoniae, Venice, 1597; St Mark's Basilica
description: This short piece from Gabrieli's Sacrae symphoniae of 1597 is scored for two instrumental groups, one led by a cornett and the other by a violin, each with trombones. It was written for the galleries of St Mark's in Venice, where the groups would have answered each other across the space. Its title refers to the dynamic markings piano and forte, which show where one group plays softly alone and where both join loudly. It is among the earliest pieces to call for particular instruments and among the first to mark dynamics, though such practices may have been older. It is a favourite of modern brass ensembles and a landmark in the rise of independent instrumental music.

title: L'Orfeo
creator: Claudio Monteverdi
type: Opera (favola in musica), prologue and five acts
location: Ducal palace, Mantua, 24 February 1607
description: L'Orfeo, with a libretto by Alessandro Striggio, was commissioned for the Accademia degli Invaghiti in Mantua during the carnival of 1607, a few years after the first Florentine operas. It tells the myth of the singer Orpheus, who descends into the underworld to reclaim his dead wife Eurydice, but loses her again when he looks back. Monteverdi combined the new recitative with songs, choruses, dances and instrumental interludes, and specified an unusually rich orchestra, including strings, brass, recorders, organ, harpsichords and plucked instruments, to create different colours for the pastoral world and Hades. The centrepiece is Orpheus's florid plea to the ferryman Charon, Possente spirto. The score was printed in 1609 and 1615, which helped it survive. Revived in the twentieth century, it is the first opera to remain in the repertoire.

title: Vespers of 1610 (Vespro della Beata Vergine)
creator: Claudio Monteverdi
type: Sacred collection for voices and instruments
location: Published in Venice, 1610, dedicated to Pope Paul V
description: Monteverdi published this collection in Venice in 1610 together with a conservative mass, dedicating them to Pope Paul V, perhaps hoping for a post in Rome. It includes music for Vespers on feasts of the Virgin: psalms, a hymn and two Magnificats, along with motets for solo voices, a sonata in which a soprano repeatedly sings Sancta Maria over instruments, and the echo piece Audi coelum. Plainchant runs through many movements as a structural thread, while around it Monteverdi deploys every modern device, from virtuoso solo singing and dance rhythms to grand choral and instrumental writing. Whether it was meant to be performed as a whole is debated. Since its revival in the twentieth century it has become one of the most popular works of the period.

title: L'incoronazione di Poppea
creator: Claudio Monteverdi
location: Teatro Santi Giovanni e Paolo, Venice, carnival 1643
description: Written for the public opera houses of Venice at the end of Monteverdi's life, to a libretto by Giovanni Francesco Busenello, Poppea tells how the Roman emperor Nero sets aside his wife Ottavia and the counsel of the philosopher Seneca to crown his mistress Poppea empress. It is one of the first operas on a historical subject, and it ends with the lovers' rapturous duet Pur ti miro, while the noble characters are exiled or dead. The music mixes recitative, arioso and songs to portray a wide range of characters, comic and tragic. The two surviving scores, from Venice and Naples, differ, and parts of the music, including probably the final duet, are by younger composers, a question of authorship that remains debated. Poppea is now regularly staged.

title: Armide
creator: Jean-Baptiste Lully
type: Tragédie en musique, prologue and five acts
location: Paris Opéra (Théâtre du Palais-Royal), 15 February 1686
description: Armide is based on Tasso's epic Jerusalem Delivered and tells of the sorceress Armide, who captures the crusader knight Renaud intending to kill him but falls in love with him instead. When he is rescued and leaves her, she destroys her enchanted palace in despair. Its libretto is by Philippe Quinault, and it was the last of their tragédies en musique. Armide's monologue Enfin il est en ma puissance, in which she hesitates over the sleeping Renaud, was admired by Rameau and Rousseau for the way recitative follows French speech. The work includes celebrated dances, such as a passacaille. Gluck later set the same libretto in 1777, a sign of its prestige.

title: Dido and Aeneas
creator: Henry Purcell
location: Josias Priest's girls' school, Chelsea, London (performance documented 1689)
description: Dido and Aeneas, with a libretto by Nahum Tate after Virgil's Aeneid, was performed at a girls' boarding school in Chelsea run by the dancing master Josias Priest in 1689, though it may have been written earlier for the court. In under an hour it tells how Aeneas, the Trojan prince, loves Dido, Queen of Carthage, until witches trick him into leaving, and Dido dies of grief. Purcell's setting of English is supple and direct, and the score includes choruses, dances and comic witch scenes. Dido's final lament unfolds over a descending chromatic ground bass repeated eleven times. No score survives from Purcell's lifetime, and the earliest copies date from decades after his death, so some music, including part of the ending of act two, is lost. Today it is one of the most performed Baroque operas.

title: Concerti grossi, Op. 6
creator: Arcangelo Corelli
location: Published by Estienne Roger, Amsterdam, 1714; many performed in Rome from the 1680s
description: Corelli's Op. 6 was published in Amsterdam in 1714, a year after his death, but many of the concertos had been played in Rome for years; the German composer Georg Muffat heard some there in 1682. In the concerto grosso a small group of soloists, two violins and a cello, alternates and blends with the full string orchestra. The first eight concertos follow the serious church sonata style, and the last four the lighter chamber style, with dance movements. No. 8 in G minor, marked 'made for the night of Christmas', ends with a gentle pastorale. The set was reprinted throughout the eighteenth century and became the model for Handel's Op. 6 and countless others.

title: Water Music
creator: George Frideric Handel
location: On barges on the River Thames, London, 17 July 1717
description: On 17 July 1717 King George I and his courtiers travelled up the Thames from Whitehall to Chelsea on a barge, while some fifty musicians played Handel's music from another barge nearby. A newspaper reported that the king liked it so much that he had it repeated three times. The music, later grouped into three suites in F, D and G, consists of overtures, airs, minuets, hornpipes and bourrées. Horns and trumpets, which carried well outdoors, give the F and D major suites their brilliance. The story that the music reconciled Handel with the king, who was annoyed that he had abandoned his post in Hanover, is a later legend. Published in parts from 1733, the Water Music has remained one of Handel's most popular works.

title: Cello Suites
creator: Johann Sebastian Bach
type: Six suites for unaccompanied cello, BWV 1007–1012
location: Copy by Anna Magdalena Bach, c. 1727–31 (no autograph survives)
description: Bach probably wrote the six suites for unaccompanied cello at Köthen, where the court orchestra had capable string players. Each opens with a prelude followed by a sequence of Baroque dances: allemande, courante, sarabande, a pair of minuets, bourrées or gavottes, and gigue. A single instrument suggests harmony and counterpoint through broken chords and implied voices. The fifth suite requires the top string to be retuned, and the sixth was written for an instrument with five strings. No autograph survives; the main sources are copies by Bach's second wife Anna Magdalena and others. Long regarded as études, the suites were made famous by the Catalan cellist Pablo Casals, who discovered an edition as a teenager and recorded them in 1936–39.

title: Brandenburg Concertos
creator: Johann Sebastian Bach
location: Autograph dedication to Margrave Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg, 24 March 1721; Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin
description: In 1721 Bach sent a beautifully copied set of six concertos to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg, whom he had met in Berlin, with a dedication in French, perhaps hoping for a post. Most of the music had been written earlier at Weimar and Köthen. Each concerto uses a different combination: No. 2 has a high trumpet, recorder, oboe and violin as soloists; No. 3 is for three groups of strings; No. 5 gives the harpsichord a long solo cadenza, a novelty that points towards the keyboard concerto; No. 6 omits violins altogether. Bach combines the Italian concerto forms of Vivaldi with dense German counterpoint. There is no record that the margrave ever had them played, and the manuscript was rediscovered in the nineteenth century and first published in 1850. They are now among Bach's most popular works.

title: The Well-Tempered Clavier
creator: Johann Sebastian Bach
location: Autograph of Book I (1722), Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin; Book II autograph in the British Library
description: Bach compiled the first book of Das wohltemperirte Clavier in 1722 at Köthen, 'for the use and profit of musical youth', and a second book around 1742 in Leipzig. Each book has a prelude and fugue in each of the twenty-four major and minor keys, rising chromatically from C major. Playing in all keys required a tuning system in which all keys sounded acceptable; the term 'well-tempered' probably refers to one of several such tunings rather than modern equal temperament, a point still discussed. The preludes range from simple broken chords, as in the famous C major prelude, to toccatas and dances; the fugues show every variety of contrapuntal technique. The collection circulated in manuscript and was published only in 1801. Mozart, Beethoven, Chopin and generations of pianists studied it, and the conductor Hans von Bülow called it the Old Testament of music.

title: Giulio Cesare in Egitto
creator: George Frideric Handel
location: King's Theatre, Haymarket, London, 20 February 1724
description: Written for the Royal Academy of Music, the London opera company Handel directed, Giulio Cesare tells of Julius Caesar's arrival in Egypt after his victory over Pompey and his affair with Cleopatra, who schemes against her brother Ptolemy. The libretto by Nicola Haym is full of intrigue and contrasting emotions, giving rise to a series of magnificent arias. The title role was written for the celebrated castrato Senesino and Cleopatra for the soprano Francesca Cuzzoni. Cleopatra's arias, including V'adoro, pupille, accompanied by an on-stage band, and the lament Piangerò la sorte mia, are among Handel's finest. The opera was a great success in its time. After two centuries of neglect, it led the revival of Handel's operas from the 1920s onwards.

title: The Four Seasons (Le quattro stagioni)
creator: Antonio Vivaldi
location: Published in Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione, Op. 8, Amsterdam, 1725
description: The Four Seasons are the first four concertos of Vivaldi's Op. 8, published in Amsterdam in 1725 under the title The Contest between Harmony and Invention, but probably written several years earlier, perhaps in Mantua. Each concerto in three movements is accompanied by a sonnet, possibly by Vivaldi himself, and letters in the score link lines of poetry to musical details: birdsong in Spring, a barking dog, a summer storm, drunken peasants and hunting in Autumn, chattering teeth and slipping on ice in Winter. The vivid pictorialism fits within ritornello form, and the solo violin part is brilliant. The works were popular in Vivaldi's time but forgotten later; after a recording revival from the 1940s they became among the most recorded pieces of classical music.

title: St Matthew Passion
creator: Johann Sebastian Bach
location: St Thomas Church, Leipzig, Good Friday, probably 11 April 1727
description: The St Matthew Passion was first performed on Good Friday in St Thomas Church, Leipzig, probably in 1727, and revised in 1736. It sets chapters 26 and 27 of Matthew's Gospel, sung by the tenor Evangelist and other soloists, with Jesus' words surrounded by a halo of sustained strings. Between the gospel narrative come reflective arias and choruses to poetry by Picander, and Lutheran chorales sung by the congregation's representative, the choir. The work uses two choirs and two orchestras, and opens with a vast chorus in which a boys' choir sings a chorale above them. Bach's own beautifully written autograph of 1736, with the gospel text in red ink, survives. After Bach's death the Passion was not heard until Felix Mendelssohn conducted it in Berlin on 11 March 1829, a performance that launched the Bach revival.

title: Hippolyte et Aricie
creator: Jean-Philippe Rameau
type: Tragédie en musique, prologue and five acts
location: Paris Opéra (Académie Royale de Musique), 1 October 1733
description: Rameau was fifty when this opera, with a libretto by the Abbé Simon-Joseph Pellegrin after Racine's Phèdre, was staged in Paris in 1733. It tells of the love of Hippolyte, son of Theseus, and Aricie, threatened by the jealousy of his stepmother Phèdre. While keeping Lully's form of the tragédie en musique, Rameau brought a new richness of harmony and orchestration, with vivid instrumental scenes such as a storm and a hunt. The second trio of the Fates was so difficult that the orchestra could not perform it as written. The work provoked a dispute between the supporters of Rameau, the 'Ramistes', and the defenders of Lully, the 'Lullistes'. It remains a centrepiece of the French Baroque revival.

title: Goldberg Variations
creator: Johann Sebastian Bach
type: Aria with thirty variations for harpsichord, BWV 988
location: Published by Balthasar Schmid, Nuremberg, 1741
description: Bach published this work in 1741 as the fourth part of his Clavier-Übung, an aria with different variations for harpsichord with two manuals. According to his early biographer Forkel, it was written for Count Keyserlingk, who suffered from insomnia, and played by his harpsichordist Johann Gottlieb Goldberg; the story is doubted, as Goldberg was then only about fourteen. The thirty variations are built on the bass line of the opening sarabande. Every third variation is a canon at increasing intervals, from the unison to the ninth, and others are virtuoso showpieces or slow laments; the last is a quodlibet combining folk songs, before the aria returns. Glenn Gould's 1955 recording made the work famous.

title: Messiah
creator: George Frideric Handel
location: Great Music Hall, Fishamble Street, Dublin, 13 April 1742
description: Handel composed Messiah in about three and a half weeks in August and September 1741, to a libretto compiled from the King James Bible and the Book of Common Prayer by Charles Jennens. It was first performed in Dublin on 13 April 1742 as a charity concert, to an audience so eager that ladies were asked not to wear hoops in their dresses. Unlike Handel's other oratorios, it has no dramatic characters; its three parts reflect on the prophecy and birth of Christ, his passion and resurrection, and the redemption of the world. Choruses such as 'For unto us a child is born' and 'Hallelujah' alternate with arias like 'I know that my Redeemer liveth'. London received it coolly at first, but annual charity performances for the Foundling Hospital from 1750 made it popular. The custom of standing for the Hallelujah chorus is traditionally linked to George II, though there is no contemporary evidence for this. Messiah has never left the repertoire.

title: Mass in B minor
creator: Johann Sebastian Bach
location: Kyrie and Gloria presented to the Elector of Saxony, Dresden, 1733; first complete performance 1859
description: In 1733 Bach presented a Kyrie and Gloria to the new Elector of Saxony in Dresden, seeking a court title. Near the end of his life, around 1748–49, he expanded it into a complete setting of the Latin Mass, writing new music and adapting movements from earlier cantatas, a process called parody. The result has twenty-seven movements for soloists, choir and orchestra, ranging from the archaic counterpoint of the Credo's opening, based on plainchant, to the dancing Gloria and the radiant Sanctus. Why a Lutheran composer completed a full Catholic mass is debated; it may have been a summation of his art, written with no particular performance in mind. It was not performed complete until 1859, and the Swiss publisher Hans Georg Nägeli called it the greatest musical work of all times and peoples.

title: Music for the Royal Fireworks
creator: George Frideric Handel
location: Green Park, London, 27 April 1749 (public rehearsal at Vauxhall Gardens, 21 April)
description: George II commissioned this music to accompany a fireworks display in Green Park celebrating the Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle, which ended the War of the Austrian Succession. The king wanted only military instruments, so Handel scored it for a large band of 24 oboes, 12 bassoons, 9 trumpets, 9 horns and timpani, adding strings later for concert performance. A public rehearsal at Vauxhall Gardens on 21 April reportedly drew 12,000 people and caused a traffic jam on London Bridge. At the display itself, part of the elaborate wooden structure caught fire. The suite consists of an overture, a bourrée, La paix, La réjouissance and two minuets.

title: The Art of Fugue
creator: Johann Sebastian Bach
type: Collection of fugues and canons, BWV 1080
location: Published posthumously, Leipzig, 1751
description: Bach worked on The Art of Fugue in his last decade. It consists of some fourteen fugues, called contrapuncti, and four canons, all derived from a single theme in D minor, presented in increasingly complex forms: in inversion, augmentation, mirror forms that can be played upside down, and multiple subjects. No instrumentation is specified. The final fugue, which introduces the notes B-A-C-H (B flat, A, C, B natural in German naming) as a subject, breaks off. A note by his son Carl Philipp Emanuel says the composer died during its writing, though scholars think it was interrupted earlier. Published in 1751, it sold few copies, but it is now regarded as one of the summits of contrapuntal art.

title: Orfeo ed Euridice
creator: Christoph Willibald Gluck
location: Burgtheater, Vienna, 5 October 1762
description: Gluck's Orfeo, with a libretto by Ranieri de' Calzabigi, retells the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice in a simple, concentrated form with only three singers and a chorus. The title role was written for the alto castrato Gaetano Guadagni. In place of long da capo arias and showy ornamentation, Gluck used orchestrally accompanied recitative, choruses, dances and simple, expressive airs. The scene in which Orpheus calms the Furies at the gates of Hades and the Dance of the Blessed Spirits are famous. The opera ends happily, as Amor restores Eurydice. Gluck revised it for Paris in 1774, for a high tenor, and in 1859 Berlioz prepared an influential edition for the mezzo-soprano Pauline Viardot. Che farò senza Euridice is one of the most famous arias of the eighteenth century.

title: Piano Concerto No. 20 in D minor
creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
location: Mehlgrube Casino, Vienna, 11 February 1785, with Mozart as soloist
description: Mozart wrote a series of piano concertos for his subscription concerts in Vienna in the 1780s, and this was the first in a minor key. The orchestra opens with quiet syncopated unease in the strings and menacing rumblings in the bass, before the soloist enters with a new, plaintive theme. The slow movement, a Romance, is serene but has a stormy central section, and the finale returns to D minor before ending in D major. Leopold Mozart heard the premiere and wrote that the concerto was magnificent; Mozart had finished copying the parts only on the day. Beethoven admired the work and wrote cadenzas for it, and in the nineteenth century it was one of the few Mozart concertos that stayed in the repertoire.

title: The Marriage of Figaro (Le nozze di Figaro)
creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
location: Burgtheater, Vienna, 1 May 1786
description: The Marriage of Figaro was the first of Mozart's three operas with the librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte. It is based on Beaumarchais's play of 1784, which had been banned in Vienna for its mockery of the aristocracy; Da Ponte toned down the politics to win the emperor's approval. Over one day, the servants Figaro and Susanna outwit their master, Count Almaviva, who wants to exercise his feudal claim on Susanna before her wedding, with the help of the neglected Countess and the lovesick page Cherubino. Mozart's ensembles, especially the long finales of acts two and four, follow the comic action and the characters' shifting emotions in continuous music. The Countess's arias and the final scene of forgiveness give the comedy unexpected depth. The opera was more successful in Prague than in Vienna, leading to the commission of Don Giovanni. It is one of the most performed operas in the world.

title: Don Giovanni
creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
location: Estates Theatre (National Theatre), Prague, 29 October 1787
description: Commissioned for Prague after the success of Figaro there, Don Giovanni was again written with Da Ponte. It opens with Don Giovanni killing the Commendatore, father of Donna Anna, whom he has tried to seduce, and follows his further conquests and evasions, with his servant Leporello cataloguing his 2,065 lovers in a famous aria. In the final scene the Commendatore's statue, which Giovanni has mockingly invited to dinner, arrives and drags the unrepentant libertine down to hell, announced by the trombones and the dark D minor music of the overture. Mozart blends comedy and tragedy, which Da Ponte's subtitle dramma giocoso reflects. For the Romantics, from E. T. A. Hoffmann to Kierkegaard, it was the opera of operas. The autograph score is in the Bibliothèque nationale de France.

title: Eine kleine Nachtmusik
creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
location: Entered in Mozart's catalogue, Vienna, 10 August 1787; published c. 1827
description: Mozart entered this serenade in his own catalogue of works on 10 August 1787, while he was writing Don Giovanni. The title simply means 'a little serenade'. Why he wrote it is unknown, and it was published only after his death. It is scored for string quartet with double bass or string orchestra and has four movements, a brisk Allegro, a gentle Romanze, a minuet and a lively rondo; Mozart's catalogue lists a second minuet that is now lost. Its perfect balance and unforgettable melodies have made it one of the most familiar pieces in classical music, endlessly used in films and advertising.

title: Symphony No. 41 in C major, 'Jupiter'
creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
location: Composed in Vienna, August 1788; first performance date uncertain
description: In the summer of 1788 Mozart wrote his last three symphonies, Nos. 39, 40 and 41, in about six weeks. Whether they were performed in his lifetime is uncertain, though it is likely. The nickname Jupiter was given later, probably by the London impresario Salomon, reflecting the grandeur of the work. Its four movements combine festive C major brilliance with operatic contrasts. The finale is a marvel of contrapuntal skill: its opening four-note motif, a chant formula used in many earlier works, and four other themes are developed in fugal textures, and in the coda all five are combined at once. It is often seen as the culmination of the eighteenth-century symphony.

title: The Magic Flute (Die Zauberflöte)
creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
location: Theater auf der Wieden, Vienna, 30 September 1791
description: The Magic Flute was written for Emanuel Schikaneder's popular suburban theatre in Vienna; Schikaneder wrote the libretto and played the bird-catcher Papageno. In its fairy-tale plot, the prince Tamino is sent by the Queen of the Night to rescue her daughter Pamina from the priest Sarastro, only to discover that Sarastro represents wisdom and that the Queen is the villain. Tamino and Pamina undergo trials of silence, fire and water to enter Sarastro's brotherhood, while Papageno finds his Papagena. The work is filled with Masonic symbolism, as both Mozart and Schikaneder were Freemasons. Musically it ranges from folk-like songs to Bachian chorales and the Queen of the Night's astonishing coloratura, rising to high F. A popular success from the start, it was Mozart's last opera, staged ten weeks before his death.

title: Requiem in D minor
creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
location: Commissioned anonymously by Count Franz von Walsegg; first performed in Vienna, 2 January 1793 (benefit for Constanze Mozart)
description: In the summer of 1791 Mozart received an anonymous commission for a requiem. The patron, Count Franz von Walsegg, intended to pass it off as his own composition in memory of his wife. When Mozart died in December, only the opening Introit was complete; for the following movements up to the Offertory he had written the vocal parts and bass line with indications for the orchestra, and the Lacrimosa broke off after eight bars. His widow Constanze, needing the fee, had the work finished, first by Joseph Eybler and then by Mozart's pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr, who claimed to have composed the Sanctus, Benedictus and Agnus Dei. How much of these sections reflects Mozart's own sketches is debated, and many modern scholars have produced alternative completions. The dark colours of basset horns and trombones and the dramatic Dies irae make it one of the best-loved choral works, surrounded by legends of a mysterious messenger and poisoning.

title: Symphony No. 94 in G major, 'Surprise'
creator: Joseph Haydn
location: Hanover Square Rooms, London, 23 March 1792
description: Haydn wrote this symphony for the second of his London seasons organised by the violinist and impresario Johann Peter Salomon. Its nickname comes from the slow movement: a simple, quiet theme is repeated even more softly and then interrupted by a loud chord with a stroke of the timpani. The story that this was meant to wake dozing audiences was popularised later; Haydn said he wanted to make a sensation with something new. The movement continues as a set of variations. The first movement begins with a slow introduction and has a lively, dance-like main section, and the minuet is a brisk peasant dance. The symphony was an immediate success and remains among his most popular.

title: String Quartets, Op. 76
creator: Joseph Haydn
location: Published in Vienna and London, 1799; dedicated to Count Joseph Erdődy
description: Haydn wrote these six quartets in 1796–97 for Count Joseph Erdődy, after his return from London; they were the last complete set he finished. They show his mastery of the genre he did more than anyone to create: dialogue between four equal instruments, motivic development and surprising harmonic turns. No. 2 is called the 'Fifths' for its opening intervals, No. 4 the 'Sunrise' for its rising first theme, and No. 3 the 'Emperor', because its slow movement is a set of variations on the hymn Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser, which Haydn had written in 1797 as an anthem for Emperor Francis II. That melody later became the tune of the German national anthem. The set has been central to the quartet repertoire ever since.

title: The Creation (Die Schöpfung)
creator: Joseph Haydn
location: Schwarzenberg Palace, Vienna, 29–30 April 1798 (private); Burgtheater, 19 March 1799 (public)
description: Inspired by the Handel oratorios he heard in London, Haydn composed The Creation to a German text adapted by Baron Gottfried van Swieten from an English libretto based on Genesis and Milton's Paradise Lost. It was published in 1800 with German and English texts. The work opens with an orchestral portrait of chaos, with hesitant, unresolved harmonies, before the chorus sings 'And there was light' on a blazing C major chord. The three archangels then narrate the six days of creation, with vivid musical pictures of storms, whales, lions and birds, and the final part celebrates Adam and Eve in Eden. A performance in Vienna in 1808, the composer's last public appearance, was a great tribute to the old Haydn.

title: Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, 'Moonlight'
creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
location: Published in Vienna, 1802; dedicated to Countess Giulietta Guicciardi
description: Beethoven subtitled this sonata 'quasi una fantasia', a sonata in the manner of a fantasy, because it departs from the usual order of movements: it opens not with a fast sonata-form movement but with a slow, quiet Adagio sostenuto in triplets, to be played with the dampers raised. A gentle Allegretto follows, and the sonata ends with a stormy Presto agitato. It was dedicated to his pupil Giulietta Guicciardi, with whom he was briefly in love. The nickname Moonlight comes from the poet Ludwig Rellstab, who after Beethoven's death compared the first movement to moonlight on Lake Lucerne. It is one of the most popular piano works ever written.

title: Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, 'Eroica'
creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
location: Lobkowitz Palace, Vienna (private), 1804; Theater an der Wien, 7 April 1805 (public)
description: Beethoven wrote the Third Symphony in 1803–04, soon after the Heiligenstadt crisis over his deafness. He originally intended to dedicate it to Napoleon Bonaparte, whom he admired as a champion of revolutionary ideals, but according to his pupil Ferdinand Ries, when he learned that Napoleon had declared himself emperor, he tore up the title page in anger. A surviving copy of the score has Napoleon's name scratched out so violently that it tore a hole in the paper. It was published as the 'heroic symphony, composed to celebrate the memory of a great man'. Its first movement, almost twice as long as any previous symphonic opening movement, develops its material with violent off-beat chords and clashing dissonances; the second is a funeral march, and the finale is a set of variations on a theme from his ballet Prometheus. It marked a turning point in the history of the symphony.

title: Symphony No. 5 in C minor
creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
location: Theater an der Wien, Vienna, 22 December 1808
description: The Fifth Symphony was first performed at a marathon concert in an unheated theatre in Vienna on 22 December 1808, together with the Sixth Symphony, the Fourth Piano Concerto and the Choral Fantasy. Its opening motif of three short notes and a long one dominates the first movement and recurs in different forms throughout. Beethoven's secretary Anton Schindler claimed he called it fate knocking at the door, but Schindler is an unreliable source. The scherzo leads without a break, through a long, eerie transition, into a blazing C major finale, where trombones, piccolo and contrabassoon make their first appearance in a symphony. The Romantic writer E. T. A. Hoffmann wrote a famous review praising its sublime, infinite longing. During the Second World War its opening, which resembles the Morse code for V, was used by the BBC as a symbol of victory.

title: Fidelio
creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
location: Theater an der Wien, Vienna, 20 November 1805; revised version Kärntnertortheater, 23 May 1814
description: Fidelio is based on a French libretto about a true story from the time of the French Revolution. Leonore, disguised as a young man named Fidelio, works as an assistant to the jailer Rocco to free her husband Florestan, a political prisoner held in a dungeon by the tyrant Pizarro. The first version, staged in 1805 just after Napoleon's troops had occupied Vienna, was a failure, and Beethoven revised it in 1806 and again thoroughly in 1814, when it succeeded. He wrote four overtures for it, three called Leonore. The prisoners' chorus, as they come out into the light, and Florestan's dungeon aria are central moments. With its celebration of freedom and marital love, Fidelio has been performed at symbolic occasions, such as the reopening of the Vienna State Opera in 1955.

title: Erlkönig
creator: Franz Schubert
location: Published as Op. 1, Vienna, 1821; first public performance 7 March 1821
description: Schubert was seventeen when he set Goethe's ballad of a father riding through the night with his sick child, who is lured and finally killed by the supernatural Erl-King. According to his friend Joseph von Spaun, he wrote it in one afternoon. The piano part hammers out the galloping hooves in relentless repeated octaves, and the single singer has to portray four characters, the narrator, the frightened child, the reassuring father and the seductive Erl-King, in different registers and styles. The child's cries rise in pitch each time, and at the end the music stops for the stark final line. Goethe was reportedly indifferent to it, but it became Schubert's first published work and made his name.

title: The Barber of Seville (Il barbiere di Siviglia)
creator: Gioachino Rossini
location: Teatro Argentina, Rome, 20 February 1816
description: Rossini wrote The Barber of Seville in a few weeks, to a libretto by Cesare Sterbini based on Beaumarchais's comedy, the prequel to The Marriage of Figaro. Count Almaviva, with the help of the resourceful barber Figaro, wins the ward Rosina from her guardian, Dr Bartolo, who wants to marry her himself. The premiere was a fiasco, disrupted by supporters of the composer Giovanni Paisiello, whose earlier opera on the same story was popular, and by stage accidents, but the second night was a triumph. The overture had been used in two earlier operas. With its patter songs, comic ensembles and crescendos, and arias such as Figaro's Largo al factotum and Rosina's Una voce poco fa, it has never left the stage.

title: Piano Sonata No. 29 in B-flat major, 'Hammerklavier'
creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
location: Published in Vienna by Artaria, 1819; dedicated to Archduke Rudolph
description: The Hammerklavier Sonata, named after the German word for the piano, was written in 1817–18 and dedicated to Beethoven's pupil and patron Archduke Rudolph. Beethoven predicted that pianists would be playing it fifty years later, and his metronome marking for the first movement is so fast that many performers consider it impractical. Its four movements last around forty-five minutes: a heroic opening Allegro, a brief scherzo, a vast and profound slow movement, and, after a hesitant introduction, a gigantic fugue full of trills and leaps that marks the extreme of Beethoven's late style. For much of the nineteenth century it was considered almost unplayable, until Liszt and Clara Schumann championed it.

title: Symphony No. 8 in B minor, 'Unfinished'
creator: Franz Schubert
location: Vienna, 17 December 1865, conducted by Johann von Herbeck
description: Schubert wrote two movements of this symphony in 1822 and sketched a third, a scherzo, in piano score, but never finished it. Why he abandoned it is unknown; theories include his illness, painful associations or the feeling that the two movements were complete. He gave the manuscript to his friend Anselm Hüttenbrenner, who kept it until 1865, when the conductor Johann von Herbeck persuaded him to release it for the premiere. The opening, with a hushed theme in the cellos and basses and a lyrical second theme, and the slow movement in E major are full of poignant contrasts. Some musicologists believe the entr'acte from Rosamunde was originally the finale. It is one of the most popular symphonies.

title: Missa solemnis in D major
creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
location: Saint Petersburg, 7 April 1824 (first complete performance); parts given in Vienna, May 1824
description: Beethoven began the Missa solemnis for the enthronement of his patron Archduke Rudolph as Archbishop of Olmütz in March 1820, but finished it three years too late. Its first complete performance took place in Saint Petersburg in 1824, sponsored by Prince Nikolai Galitzin, and three movements were heard in Vienna at the premiere of the Ninth Symphony. Above the Kyrie Beethoven wrote 'From the heart, may it go again to the heart'. He studied old church music and the Latin text closely, and the work is full of personal emphasis, from the fugues of the Gloria and Credo to the violin solo that descends from heaven in the Benedictus and the military sounds that interrupt the plea for peace in the Agnus Dei. He considered it his greatest work.

title: Symphony No. 9 in D minor, 'Choral'
creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
location: Theater am Kärntnertor, Vienna, 7 May 1824
description: Beethoven had long wanted to set Friedrich Schiller's poem An die Freude, and in the Ninth Symphony, commissioned in part by the Philharmonic Society of London, he did so in a finale for four soloists, chorus and orchestra. The first three movements, a mysterious opening that emerges from empty fifths, a driving scherzo and a serene slow movement, are recalled and rejected at the start of the finale, before the cellos and basses introduce the joy theme. Its variations include a Turkish march and a solemn hymn to the creator above the stars. At the premiere the totally deaf composer stood beside the conductor, and it is said that one of the soloists had to turn him round to see the audience's applause. The joy melody became the anthem of the European Union, and the autograph is listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

title: String Quartet No. 14 in C-sharp minor
creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
location: Published posthumously, Mainz, 1827; first public performance 1835
description: Beethoven's last five string quartets, written in 1825–26 after the Ninth Symphony, explored new forms and expressive extremes that puzzled contemporaries. The C-sharp minor Quartet, Op. 131, has seven movements played continuously, beginning with a slow, mournful fugue that Wagner called the saddest thing ever expressed in notes. Beethoven is said to have regarded it as his greatest quartet, and Schubert asked to hear it on his deathbed, according to a story told by a friend. A theme and variations forms its centre, and the work ends with a furious finale that recalls the opening fugue. The late quartets have been a source of wonder and study for composers ever since, from Wagner to Bartók and Shostakovich.

title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
creator: Felix Mendelssohn
type: Concert overture, Op. 21, and incidental music, Op. 61
location: Overture first performed Stettin, 20 February 1827; incidental music Neues Palais, Potsdam, 14 October 1843
description: Mendelssohn wrote the concert overture to Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream at seventeen, after reading the play in German translation with his sister Fanny. Four wind chords open the door to fairyland, and rapid, light string music evokes the fairies, while later themes portray the lovers, the court, and Bottom's braying as a donkey. In 1843, at the request of King Frederick William IV of Prussia, he wrote incidental music for a staging of the play in Potsdam, including the Scherzo, Nocturne and Wedding March, and reused the overture. The Wedding March became a staple of weddings after it was played at the marriage of Queen Victoria's daughter Victoria in 1858.

title: Winterreise
creator: Franz Schubert
location: Published by Haslinger, Vienna, 1828
description: Schubert set twenty-four poems by Wilhelm Müller in Winterreise (Winter Journey), composed in two parts in 1827, during his last illness. A young man, rejected in love, leaves town at night and wanders through a frozen landscape, encountering a weathervane, a frozen river, a crow, a signpost and a graveyard. The cycle ends with an old hurdy-gurdy player, ignored by all, whose droning tune suggests a bleak future. Schubert's friends were dismayed by the sombreness of the songs when he first sang them, but he said he liked them more than all others. The piano evokes each scene with economy: the turning weathervane, the trudging steps, the hurdy-gurdy's drone. Winterreise is a summit of the song repertoire for singers.

title: String Quintet in C major
creator: Franz Schubert
location: Vienna, 17 November 1850 (first public performance); published 1853
description: Schubert completed the String Quintet in the late summer of 1828, two months before his death, and it was neither performed nor published in his lifetime. Unlike Mozart's quintets, which add a second viola, it adds a second cello, giving the sound richness and depth. The first movement is vast and lyrical; the Adagio, in which the inner voices sing a slow hymn over pizzicato bass and violin figures, is surrounded by a violent central section; the scherzo is energetic and the finale has a Hungarian character. Many musicians consider it the greatest work of chamber music, and the Adagio is often requested at funerals and played at moments of mourning.

title: Symphonie fantastique
creator: Hector Berlioz
location: Paris Conservatoire, 5 December 1830
description: Berlioz wrote the Symphonie fantastique, subtitled 'Episode in the life of an artist', in 1830, inspired by his unrequited passion for the Irish Shakespearean actress Harriet Smithson. A printed programme tells how a young musician, in despair over love, poisons himself with opium and dreams. His beloved is represented by a melody, the idée fixe, which recurs in each movement: at a ball, in a pastoral scene with shepherds' pipes and distant thunder, at his own execution in a march to the scaffold, and finally, grotesquely distorted, at a witches' sabbath that quotes the Dies irae chant. Berlioz's orchestra included cor anglais, E-flat clarinet, harps, bells and four timpani for the thunder. Smithson attended a performance in 1832, and the two married the following year. The work is a founding example of the Romantic programme symphony.

title: Nocturnes
creator: Frédéric Chopin
location: Published in Paris, Leipzig and London from 1832
description: The nocturne, a dreamy piano piece with a singing melody over broken-chord accompaniment, was invented by the Irish composer John Field, but Chopin made it his own. His twenty-one nocturnes, published mostly in sets of two or three between 1832 and 1846, with two more after his death, transfer the ornamented lines of Bellini's bel canto opera to the piano, with fluid rubato and rich harmony created by the sustaining pedal. Many have stormy middle sections that contrast with their tranquil outer parts. The Nocturne in E-flat major, Op. 9 No. 2, is among the most famous of all piano pieces, while late nocturnes such as Op. 48 No. 1 in C minor reach tragic grandeur.

title: Études, Op. 10 and Op. 25
creator: Frédéric Chopin
location: Published Paris, Leipzig and London, 1833 and 1837; Op. 10 dedicated to Liszt
description: Chopin's two sets of twelve études each focus on a particular technical problem, such as arpeggios, chromatic scales, octaves or the independence of the weak fingers, but they are also concert pieces of great expressive and musical richness. Op. 10, written largely in Warsaw and Vienna before 1832, is dedicated to Liszt, and Op. 25 to Liszt's partner Marie d'Agoult. Among the best known are the 'Revolutionary' Étude in C minor, Op. 10 No. 12, associated with the fall of Warsaw to the Russians in 1831, the lyrical Op. 10 No. 3 in E major, and the 'Winter Wind', Op. 25 No. 11. They established the étude as an artistic genre, followed by Liszt, Debussy, Scriabin and Ligeti.

title: Ballade No. 1 in G minor
creator: Frédéric Chopin
location: Published 1836; dedicated to Baron Nathaniel de Stockhausen
description: Chopin's four ballades created a new kind of piano piece: a large, single-movement narrative in which themes are transformed dramatically over the course of the music. The first, begun in Vienna around 1831 and finished in Paris, opens with a mysterious recitative-like introduction before a hesitant waltz-like theme. A lyrical second theme returns, transformed, in a radiant fortissimo, before a virtuosic and tragic coda. The ballades are often linked to the poetry of Adam Mickiewicz, Chopin's compatriot, though Chopin gave no programme. Schumann reported that Chopin told him it was his favourite among his works. It is one of the pinnacles of the Romantic piano repertoire.

title: Piano Concerto in A minor
creator: Clara Schumann
location: Leipzig Gewandhaus, 9 November 1835, with the composer as soloist and Mendelssohn conducting
description: Clara Wieck began this concerto when she was about thirteen, writing what became its finale first as a one-movement piece, possibly with help from Robert Schumann on the orchestration. She completed it in 1835 and played it at the Leipzig Gewandhaus with Mendelssohn conducting. Its three movements are linked without pauses. The slow movement is a remarkable Romanze in which the orchestra falls silent, leaving the piano in duet with a solo cello, an idea that Brahms later echoed in his Second Piano Concerto. The work shows the influence of Chopin and of the virtuoso concertos of the day. After decades of neglect, it has been recorded and performed frequently since the late twentieth century.

title: Kinderszenen
creator: Robert Schumann
location: Published Leipzig, 1839
description: Schumann wrote Kinderszenen (Scenes from Childhood) in 1838, telling Clara that they were reminiscences of childhood by a grown-up for grown-ups, and not pieces for children. The thirteen miniatures, with titles added afterwards, such as Of Foreign Lands and Peoples, Catch Me, Frightening and Child Falling Asleep, are simple in texture but subtle in harmony and in the links between pieces. The seventh, Träumerei (Dreaming), became one of the most famous piano pieces, and Vladimir Horowitz often played it as an encore. The cycle ends with The Poet Speaks, a quiet reflection. It typifies Schumann's art of poetic character pieces.

title: Dichterliebe
creator: Robert Schumann
location: Published Leipzig, 1844
description: Schumann wrote Dichterliebe (A Poet's Love) in a single week in May 1840, his 'year of song', when he finally won the legal battle to marry Clara Wieck. It sets sixteen poems from Heinrich Heine's Lyrisches Intermezzo. The cycle moves from the first song, in which love blossoms in the lovely month of May, through dreams, tears and bitter irony, to a final song in which the poet buries his love in a huge coffin. The opening song, which hovers without a firm key and ends on an unresolved chord, is famous. The piano has its own voice, with long postludes that comment on and complete the songs. Dichterliebe is one of the central song cycles of the repertoire.

title: Violin Concerto in E minor
creator: Felix Mendelssohn
location: Leipzig Gewandhaus, 13 March 1845, with Ferdinand David as soloist
description: Mendelssohn promised a concerto to his friend Ferdinand David, leader of the Gewandhaus Orchestra, in 1838 and completed it in 1844 after long consultation with him. Its innovations include the soloist's immediate entry without an orchestral introduction, the placing of the cadenza before the recapitulation rather than near the end of the first movement, and the linking of all three movements without pauses, with a single bassoon note leading to the slow movement. The finale is a sparkling, elfin rondo. The concerto quickly became a cornerstone of the violin repertoire.

title: Rigoletto
creator: Giuseppe Verdi
location: Teatro La Fenice, Venice, 11 March 1851
description: Rigoletto is based on Victor Hugo's play Le roi s'amuse, which had been banned in France after one performance. The Austrian censors in Venice objected to the depiction of a licentious king, so Verdi and his librettist Francesco Maria Piave changed the setting to the court of the Duke of Mantua. The jester Rigoletto mocks the victims of his master, the womanising Duke, but is cursed by one of them, the Count Monterone. When the Duke seduces Rigoletto's daughter Gilda, Rigoletto hires an assassin, but Gilda sacrifices herself for the Duke. Verdi's dramatic treatment, including the storm scene and the famous quartet in which four characters express different emotions simultaneously, marked a new stage in his career. The Duke's carefree 'La donna è mobile' was so catchy that Verdi kept it secret until the final rehearsal.

title: Piano Sonata in B minor
creator: Franz Liszt
location: Published 1854; dedicated to Robert Schumann; first public performance Berlin, 27 January 1857, by Hans von Bülow
description: Liszt completed his only piano sonata in Weimar in 1853 and dedicated it to Robert Schumann, who had dedicated his Fantasy in C to Liszt. Its four main sections, corresponding to the movements of a traditional sonata, are fused into a single continuous movement lasting about thirty minutes, and a handful of themes, such as a descending scale, a hammered motif and a grand chorale, are transformed into new characters throughout. Brahms reportedly fell asleep when Liszt played it to him, and the critic Hanslick condemned it, but Wagner was enthusiastic. Its formal invention influenced later composers, and it is now considered one of the summits of the piano repertoire.

title: La traviata
creator: Giuseppe Verdi
location: Teatro La Fenice, Venice, 6 March 1853
description: La traviata (The Fallen Woman) is based on the play by Alexandre Dumas fils, which Verdi saw in Paris, drawn from the life of the courtesan Marie Duplessis. Violetta Valéry, a courtesan suffering from tuberculosis, gives up her life of pleasure for the young Alfredo Germont, but his father persuades her to leave him to protect his family's reputation. Alfredo publicly insults her, and the lovers are reunited only as she dies. Unusually for its time, the opera dealt with a contemporary subject, though the censors had it set in the early eighteenth century. The premiere failed, partly because of casting, but a revised production in Venice in 1854 was a success. With its brindisi drinking song, Violetta's 'Sempre libera' and the delicate preludes, it is now one of the most performed operas in the world.

title: Les préludes
creator: Franz Liszt
location: Weimar Court Theatre, 23 February 1854, conducted by Liszt
description: Les préludes is the third of Liszt's thirteen symphonic poems, one-movement orchestral works inspired by literature or art. It originated as the overture to an unfinished choral work, and Liszt later connected it to a poem by Alphonse de Lamartine, presenting life as a series of preludes to the unknown song of death, a link that scholars think was added after the music was written. A three-note motif is transformed through scenes of love, storm, pastoral peace and a battle-like triumph. The technique of thematic transformation influenced Wagner, Strauss and many others. The work's final fanfare was sadly misused in Nazi newsreels during the Second World War.

title: Tristan und Isolde
creator: Richard Wagner
location: Königliches Hof- und Nationaltheater, Munich, 10 June 1865, conducted by Hans von Bülow
description: Wagner interrupted his work on the Ring to write Tristan und Isolde, inspired by the medieval romance of Gottfried von Strassburg, Schopenhauer's philosophy and his own passion for Mathilde Wesendonck, the wife of a patron. Isolde, an Irish princess being brought by the knight Tristan to marry King Mark of Cornwall, intends to poison herself and Tristan, but her maid substitutes a love potion. Their love can only be fulfilled in night and death. The Prelude opens with the 'Tristan chord', an ambiguous dissonance that resolves only into further dissonance, and the music yearns towards resolutions that are postponed until Isolde's final Liebestod. Tristan was considered unperformable in Vienna after dozens of rehearsals, and was premiered in Munich with Ludwig II's support. Its harmony is often seen as the beginning of the end of traditional tonality.

title: Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg
creator: Richard Wagner
location: Königliches Hof- und Nationaltheater, Munich, 21 June 1868
description: Die Meistersinger is set in sixteenth-century Nuremberg, where the shoemaker-poet Hans Sachs, a historical figure, helps the young knight Walther win a singing contest and the hand of Eva, against the pedantic town clerk Beckmesser. The work celebrates German art and the balance between tradition and innovation, and contains Wagner's most diatonic and contrapuntal music, including a famous overture that combines several themes at once. Many have seen Beckmesser as an antisemitic caricature and as a portrait of the critic Hanslick, though the extent of such meanings is debated. The Nazis made the opera a showpiece at Bayreuth, a history that later productions often confront.

title: A German Requiem (Ein deutsches Requiem)
creator: Johannes Brahms
location: Bremen Cathedral, 10 April 1868 (Good Friday); complete seven-movement version Leipzig, 18 February 1869
description: Brahms began work on A German Requiem after the death of his mother in 1865, and perhaps with Robert Schumann's death in mind. Instead of the Latin text of the Catholic requiem mass, he selected passages from Luther's German Bible about grief, transience and consolation, opening with 'Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted'. Six movements were performed in Bremen Cathedral on Good Friday 1868; Brahms then added a fifth movement for soprano solo, 'Ye now have sorrow', and the complete version was heard in 1869. The second movement, 'For all flesh is as grass', is a slow funeral march, and fugues crown several movements. The success of the work made Brahms famous across Europe.

title: Piano Concerto in A minor
creator: Edvard Grieg
location: Casino Theatre, Copenhagen, 3 April 1869, with Edmund Neupert as soloist
description: Grieg wrote his Piano Concerto at the age of twenty-four during a summer in Denmark. Its opening, a timpani roll and a cascade of chords down the keyboard, is one of the most recognisable in the repertoire, and its themes are infused with Norwegian folk rhythms and harmonies. The form follows Schumann's Piano Concerto, in the same key, which Grieg had heard in Leipzig. Liszt played through the manuscript at sight in Rome and encouraged him warmly. Grieg revised the concerto many times, until shortly before his death. It was the first piano concerto to be recorded, in a shortened version in 1909.

title: Aida
creator: Giuseppe Verdi
location: Khedivial Opera House, Cairo, 24 December 1871
description: Aida was commissioned by Isma'il Pasha, the Khedive of Egypt, for his new opera house in Cairo; the story was devised by the French Egyptologist Auguste Mariette and the libretto written by Antonio Ghislanzoni. Aida, an Ethiopian princess enslaved in Egypt, loves the Egyptian general Radamès, who is loved in turn by the Pharaoh's daughter Amneris. Radamès is tricked into betraying military secrets and is buried alive, and Aida joins him in the tomb. The opera combines grand spectacle, as in the triumphal scene with its long trumpets, with intimate drama. The Cairo premiere was delayed by the Franco-Prussian War, as the sets and costumes were trapped in besieged Paris. It is one of the most popular operas.

title: Messa da Requiem
creator: Giuseppe Verdi
location: San Marco, Milan, 22 May 1874, conducted by Verdi
description: After the death of Rossini in 1868, Verdi proposed a joint requiem by Italian composers, to which he contributed the Libera me, but the project collapsed. When the poet and novelist Alessandro Manzoni, author of The Betrothed, whom Verdi revered, died in 1873, he wrote a whole requiem in his memory, incorporating a revised version of the Libera me. It was first performed in the church of San Marco in Milan on the first anniversary of Manzoni's death. The Dies irae, with its hammer-blows on the bass drum and offstage trumpets in the Tuba mirum, became famous. Hans von Bülow called it an opera in church vestments, a judgement Brahms rejected. It is now one of the most performed choral works.

title: Boris Godunov
creator: Modest Mussorgsky
location: Mariinsky Theatre, Saint Petersburg, 8 February 1874 (revised version)
description: Mussorgsky based his opera on Pushkin's drama about Boris Godunov, who became Tsar in 1598 after the death of the young heir Dmitry, whom he is suspected of having had murdered, and on the historian Karamzin. The first version, completed in 1869, was rejected by the Imperial Theatres, partly because it lacked a major female role. Mussorgsky revised it, adding a Polish act with a love story, and it was staged in 1874. The crowd scenes, in which the Russian people are central, the coronation scene with its pealing bells, and Boris's hallucinations of guilt are powerful. After Mussorgsky's death, Rimsky-Korsakov prepared a polished version that made the opera famous; since the mid-twentieth century the composer's own versions have increasingly been preferred.

title: Pictures at an Exhibition
creator: Modest Mussorgsky
location: Composed June 1874; published 1886; Ravel's orchestration premiered in Paris, 19 October 1922
description: Mussorgsky wrote this piano suite in a few weeks in 1874 after a memorial exhibition of drawings and watercolours by his friend the artist and architect Viktor Hartmann, who had died the previous year. Ten pieces depict individual pictures, such as a gnome, an old castle, a Polish ox-cart, unhatched chicks in their shells, the witch Baba Yaga's hut on hen's legs and Hartmann's design for a great gate in Kiev. They are linked by a recurring Promenade, representing the visitor walking around the gallery. Only a few of Hartmann's pictures survive. The suite was published only after Mussorgsky's death. It became famous in Ravel's brilliant orchestration of 1922, commissioned by the conductor Serge Koussevitzky.

title: Carmen
creator: Georges Bizet
location: Opéra-Comique, Paris, 3 March 1875
description: Carmen, with a libretto by Henri Meilhac and Ludovic Halévy after Prosper Mérimée's novella, is set in Seville. Carmen, a cigarette-factory worker, seduces the soldier Don José, who deserts the army to join her and a band of smugglers. When she leaves him for the bullfighter Escamillo, José stabs her to death outside the bullring. The Opéra-Comique was a family theatre, and its directors were shocked by the realism and immorality of the story, which some critics condemned. Bizet's score is full of memorable numbers, including Carmen's Habanera, based on a song by Sebastián Yradier, the Seguidilla and the Toreador Song, and Spanish rhythms that he largely invented himself. Bizet died three months after the premiere. A version with sung recitatives by Ernest Guiraud spread the opera worldwide, and it is one of the most performed operas.

title: Der Ring des Nibelungen
creator: Richard Wagner
location: Complete cycle first performed at the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, 13–17 August 1876
description: Wagner worked on the Ring for more than a quarter of a century. He wrote the texts in reverse order, beginning with Siegfried's death, and then composed the music in order: Das Rheingold, Die Walküre, Siegfried, with a long interruption, and Götterdämmerung. The story, drawn from the Nibelungenlied and Icelandic sagas, follows a magic ring forged from stolen Rhine gold, the curse it bears, and the downfall of the gods, through the god Wotan, his daughter the Valkyrie Brünnhilde and the hero Siegfried. It was conceived as a critique of power and greed. The music is woven from a network of leitmotifs for characters, objects and ideas, such as the Ride of the Valkyries. Wagner built the Festspielhaus in Bayreuth, with its hidden orchestra pit, to stage it, and the first complete cycle in 1876 was attended by the German emperor, Tchaikovsky, Liszt and Bruckner. It is considered the most ambitious work in the history of opera.

title: Peer Gynt
creator: Edvard Grieg
type: Incidental music, Op. 23; later two suites
location: Christiania Theatre, Christiania (Oslo), 24 February 1876
description: Ibsen asked Grieg to write music for the first staging of his verse play Peer Gynt, about a boastful, wandering Norwegian peasant who seeks himself around the world and finally returns home to the faithful Solveig. Grieg found the task difficult and called some parts loathsome, but the score became one of his best-loved works. He later extracted two orchestral suites (1888 and 1891). Morning Mood, actually set in the Moroccan desert, evokes a sunrise; In the Hall of the Mountain King grows from a quiet march into a frantic dance of trolls; and Solveig's Song is a melancholy Norwegian melody. The music has become inseparable from images of Norway.

title: Swan Lake
creator: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
location: Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow, 4 March 1877; Petipa–Ivanov revival Mariinsky Theatre, Saint Petersburg, 1895
description: Tchaikovsky was commissioned to write Swan Lake by the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow. Prince Siegfried falls in love with Odette, a princess turned into a swan by the sorcerer Rothbart, who can become human only at night. At a ball, Rothbart's daughter Odile, disguised as Odette, tricks Siegfried into swearing love to her, and the lovers die. The first production was poorly received, with weak choreography and staging. After Tchaikovsky's death the choreographers Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov created a new version in Saint Petersburg in 1895, which is the basis of most later productions, with its white acts for the corps de ballet of swans. Tchaikovsky's symphonic, richly melodic score transformed ballet music, and the work is perhaps the most famous ballet in the world.

title: Violin Concerto in D major
creator: Johannes Brahms
location: Leipzig Gewandhaus, 1 January 1879, with Joseph Joachim as soloist and Brahms conducting
description: Brahms wrote this concerto for his friend Joseph Joachim, one of the leading violinists of the age, who advised him on the solo part and wrote the cadenza still most often played. It was premiered on New Year's Day 1879 in Leipzig. The orchestra plays an important symphonic role, prompting the conductor Hans von Bülow to call it a concerto against the violin rather than for it. The slow movement opens with a long oboe solo, which the violinist Pablo de Sarasate reportedly refused to stand listening to, and the finale is a vigorous rondo with a Hungarian flavour, a tribute to Joachim. With Beethoven's and Mendelssohn's it is one of the great Romantic violin concertos.

title: Eugene Onegin
creator: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
location: Maly Theatre, Moscow, by Conservatory students, 29 March 1879
description: Tchaikovsky called Eugene Onegin 'lyric scenes' rather than an opera, and it follows Pushkin's verse novel. The young Tatyana falls in love with the worldly Onegin and confesses her love in a long letter, which he coolly rejects. Onegin later kills his friend Lensky in a duel. Years later, he meets Tatyana, now married to a prince, and falls in love with her, but she refuses him. The famous Letter Scene, in which Tatyana writes through the night, was the first part Tchaikovsky composed. Written at the time of his own disastrous marriage, it was premiered by student performers at his request, because he feared the conventions of the Imperial Theatres. It is the most popular Russian opera.

title: Parsifal
creator: Richard Wagner
type: Bühnenweihfestspiel (stage consecration festival play), three acts
location: Bayreuth Festspielhaus, 26 July 1882
description: Parsifal, based on Wolfram von Eschenbach's medieval epic, tells of a guileless youth who becomes the redeemer of the Grail knights, whose king Amfortas suffers from a wound that will not heal. Through compassion and resistance to the temptation of Kundry, Parsifal recovers the sacred spear and heals the wound. Wagner called it a festival play for the consecration of the stage and wanted it performed only at Bayreuth; this exclusivity lasted until the Metropolitan Opera staged it in New York in 1903 and other houses after copyright expired in 1913. The music is slow-moving, luminous and harmonically rich. Its religious themes, its mixture of Christian and Buddhist ideas and its possible racial undertones have long been debated.

title: Má vlast
creator: Bedřich Smetana
location: Complete cycle first performed in Prague, 5 November 1882
description: Smetana composed Má vlast (My Homeland) between 1874 and 1879, mostly after he had gone completely deaf. The six symphonic poems evoke Czech land and myth: Vyšehrad, the castle of the ancient kings in Prague; Vltava, which follows the river from two springs through forests, a peasant wedding and moonlit nymphs to Prague; Šárka, the legend of a warrior maiden; From Bohemia's Woods and Fields; and Tábor and Blaník, about the Hussite warriors of the fifteenth century and their legendary return. The Hussite chorale 'Ye who are warriors of God' unites the last two. Performed complete for the first time in 1882, it became a symbol of Czech identity and opens the Prague Spring festival each year.

title: Symphony No. 7 in E major
creator: Anton Bruckner
location: Leipzig, 30 December 1884, conducted by Arthur Nikisch
description: Bruckner began his Seventh Symphony in 1881, opening it with a long, rising cello melody that he said came to him in a dream. While writing the slow movement he heard of Wagner's illness and death in Venice in February 1883, and he ended the Adagio with a funeral lament for four Wagner tubas, the instruments Wagner had designed for the Ring. The premiere in Leipzig under Arthur Nikisch and a performance in Munich under Hermann Levi brought Bruckner his first wide recognition at the age of sixty. The work is dedicated to King Ludwig II of Bavaria. Unlike several of his symphonies, it survives essentially in one version, although the cymbal clash at the climax of the Adagio is disputed.

title: Symphony No. 4 in E minor
creator: Johannes Brahms
location: Meiningen, 25 October 1885, conducted by Brahms
description: Brahms wrote his Fourth Symphony during two summers at Mürzzuschlag in the Styrian Alps and conducted the premiere with the Meiningen Court Orchestra. The first movement grows from a chain of falling thirds and rising sixths; the slow movement opens in an archaic Phrygian mode; and the third is a boisterous scherzo with a triangle. The finale is a passacaglia, thirty variations and a coda on an eight-bar theme adapted from the closing chorus of Bach's Cantata BWV 150, a rare use of a Baroque form to end a Romantic symphony. Initially some of Brahms's friends found it austere, but it is now seen as one of the summits of the symphonic tradition.

title: Otello
creator: Giuseppe Verdi
location: La Scala, Milan, 5 February 1887
description: After Aida Verdi announced his retirement, but his publisher Giulio Ricordi and the composer-poet Arrigo Boito lured him back with a libretto based on Shakespeare's Othello. Boito compressed the play, dropping the Venice act, and wrote Iago a 'Credo' in which he declares his belief in a cruel God. The opera opens in the middle of a storm and moves through continuous music, with Otello's love duet with Desdemona, his growing jealousy and the final scene, in which Desdemona sings the Willow Song and Ave Maria before Otello kills her and then himself. The premiere at La Scala was a national event. It is widely regarded as the summit of Italian tragic opera.

title: Gymnopédies
creator: Erik Satie
location: Published in Paris, 1888 (No. 1) and 1895
description: Satie wrote the three Gymnopédies in 1888 while working as a pianist in Montmartre. The title probably refers to an ancient Spartan festival at which naked young men danced, perhaps taken from a poem by his friend J. P. Contamine de Latour. Each piece has a slow, simple melody over a gently rocking accompaniment of alternating bass notes and chords, with unusual, modal harmonies.
