Their restraint and repetitiveness were the opposite of the expansive Romantic style. Debussy orchestrated the first and third in 1897. The pieces became widely known in the twentieth century, used in films and advertising, and are often cited as precursors of ambient music.

title: The Nutcracker
creator: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
location: Mariinsky Theatre, Saint Petersburg, 18 December 1892
description: The Nutcracker is based on Alexandre Dumas's adaptation of E. T. A. Hoffmann's story The Nutcracker and the Mouse King, and was choreographed by Lev Ivanov from Petipa's scenario. At a Christmas Eve party, young Clara receives a nutcracker that comes to life, battles the Mouse King and takes her to the Land of Sweets, where dances of many lands are performed. For the Sugar Plum Fairy, Tchaikovsky used the celesta, a new instrument he had discovered in Paris. The premiere, in a double bill with his opera Iolanta, was not a great success, but the suite he extracted earlier was popular. From the 1950s, especially George Balanchine's 1954 New York production, the ballet became a Christmas tradition worldwide.

title: Symphony No. 6 in B minor, 'Pathétique'
creator: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
location: Saint Petersburg, 28 October 1893, conducted by the composer
description: Tchaikovsky wrote his last symphony in 1893 and considered it the best thing he had composed. The title Pathétique, roughly 'passionate' or 'emotional' in Russian, was suggested by his brother Modest. It breaks with symphonic tradition by ending in a slow, quiet movement that fades away into darkness, after a march-like third movement whose energetic conclusion often prompts applause. The second movement is a graceful waltz in an irregular 5/4 metre. Tchaikovsky conducted the premiere nine days before his death, and the symphony has been heard as a requiem for himself, an interpretation encouraged by speculation about the circumstances of his death, though he had planned a hidden programme of his own that he never disclosed.

title: Symphony No. 9 in E minor, 'From the New World'
creator: Antonín Dvořák
location: Carnegie Hall, New York, 16 December 1893, New York Philharmonic conducted by Anton Seidl
description: Dvořák wrote the New World Symphony in New York in the first months of 1893, while directing the National Conservatory, and its premiere at Carnegie Hall was a triumph. He said he had studied African American and Native American melodies and tried to write in their spirit, though all the themes are his own; how far its idioms are American or Czech has been debated ever since. The slow movement's melody for the cor anglais was later turned into the song Goin' Home by one of his students. The finale recalls themes from all the earlier movements. Neil Armstrong reportedly took a recording to the Moon in 1969. It is one of the most popular symphonies in the world.

title: Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune
creator: Claude Debussy
location: Société Nationale de Musique, Salle d'Harcourt, Paris, 22 December 1894
description: Debussy's Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun was inspired by Stéphane Mallarmé's poem, in which a faun, half man and half goat, wakes in the heat of the afternoon and recalls, or dreams of, an encounter with nymphs. Debussy intended it as the first part of a triptych, but completed only the prelude. It opens with a sinuous, chromatic solo flute melody that slides through the interval of a tritone, unaccompanied, followed by soft harps and horns. The music develops not through traditional thematic argument but by subtle variation of colour and harmony, with flexible rhythm and a fluid form. Mallarmé was delighted. The conductor and composer Pierre Boulez said that modern music was awakened by it. In 1912 Vaslav Nijinsky choreographed it for the Ballets Russes, causing a scandal with its erotic ending.

title: Symphony No. 2 in C minor, 'Resurrection'
creator: Gustav Mahler
type: Symphony with soprano, alto and chorus
location: Berlin, 13 December 1895, Berlin Philharmonic conducted by Mahler
description: Mahler worked on his Second Symphony for six years. The first movement, originally a tone poem called Totenfeier (Funeral Rites), asks the meaning of life and death; the next three movements look back at memories of happiness, the irony of life, in an orchestral version of his song about St Anthony preaching to the fish, and simple faith, in the song Urlicht. Mahler had difficulty finding a finale until he heard Klopstock's hymn Die Auferstehung (Resurrection) at the funeral of the conductor Hans von Bülow in 1894. The finale, lasting more than half an hour, includes an offstage band, a 'great summons' of horns and birdsong, before the chorus enters almost inaudibly and builds to an overwhelming climax with organ and bells. Its premiere was Mahler's first major success as a composer.

title: La bohème
creator: Giacomo Puccini
location: Teatro Regio, Turin, 1 February 1896, conducted by Arturo Toscanini
description: La bohème, with a libretto by Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa, is based on Henri Murger's stories of bohemian life in 1840s Paris. The poet Rodolfo falls in love with his neighbour, the seamstress Mimì, when she knocks on his door for a light; their friends, the painter Marcello and the fickle Musetta, quarrel and make up. The lovers separate because Rodolfo cannot bear to watch Mimì's illness worsen in their cold garret, and she returns to die among her friends. The arias 'Che gelida manina' and 'Sì, mi chiamano Mimì', Musetta's waltz and the Café Momus scene show Puccini's gift for melody and theatrical timing. Critics were cool at the premiere, but the public loved it, and it is among the most performed operas in the world. It inspired the musical Rent.

title: Also sprach Zarathustra
creator: Richard Strauss
location: Frankfurt, 27 November 1896, conducted by Strauss
description: Strauss wrote this tone poem 'freely after Friedrich Nietzsche', inspired by Nietzsche's philosophical novel Thus Spoke Zarathustra. Its nine sections take titles from chapters of the book, such as Of the Backworldsmen, Of Joys and Passions, Of Science and the Dance Song, and trace humanity's development towards the idea of the Übermensch. The opening, a sunrise built on a low C followed by a rising trumpet fanfare of C, G and C and a blazing orchestral chord, became world-famous after Stanley Kubrick used it in 2001: A Space Odyssey in 1968. The work ends ambiguously, with B major and C major chords alternating. Strauss said he did not want to write philosophical music, but to convey in music an idea of the evolution of the human race.

title: Verklärte Nacht
creator: Arnold Schoenberg
location: Vienna, 18 March 1902, Rosé Quartet with additional players
description: Verklärte Nacht (Transfigured Night) is a one-movement string sextet, written in three weeks in 1899, based on a poem by Richard Dehmel. A woman walking with her lover through a moonlit forest confesses that she is pregnant by another man; he replies that their love will transfigure the child as their own. The music follows the poem's five stanzas, moving from D minor anguish to a radiant D major. Its harmonies, influenced by Wagner and Brahms, were too daring for the Vienna Tonkünstlerverein, which rejected it because of one supposedly non-existent chord. Schoenberg later arranged it for string orchestra, and it is his most popular work.

title: Tosca
creator: Giacomo Puccini
location: Teatro Costanzi, Rome, 14 January 1900
description: Tosca is based on Victorien Sardou's play, which Puccini had seen with Sarah Bernhardt in the title role. Its action takes place over less than a day in Rome in June 1800, during Napoleon's campaign in Italy, in real places: the church of Sant'Andrea della Valle, the Palazzo Farnese and the Castel Sant'Angelo. The singer Floria Tosca tries to save her lover, the painter Cavaradossi, from the brutal police chief Scarpia, who wants her for himself. She stabs Scarpia but is deceived: Cavaradossi's mock execution turns out to be real, and she throws herself from the castle battlements. The arias 'Vissi d'arte', 'Recondita armonia' and 'E lucevan le stelle' are famous. The musicologist Joseph Kerman dismissed it as a 'shabby little shocker', but it is one of the most popular operas.

title: Finlandia
creator: Jean Sibelius
location: Helsinki, 2 July 1900 (revised version)
description: Finlandia originated in 1899 as the final piece in music for a series of tableaux depicting Finnish history, presented at a 'press celebration' in Helsinki in protest against Russian censorship and restrictions on Finnish autonomy. Sibelius revised it as an independent work in 1900. Its brooding brass opening evokes the struggle of the Finnish people, followed by a stirring Allegro and a hymn-like central melody. Because of its political significance, it was performed under other titles to evade censorship. In 1941 Sibelius arranged the hymn for choir with words by Veikko Antero Koskenniemi, and it is often regarded as Finland's second national anthem.

title: Pelléas et Mélisande
creator: Claude Debussy
location: Opéra-Comique, Paris, 30 April 1902
description: Debussy set Maurice Maeterlinck's Symbolist play almost word for word. In the mysterious kingdom of Allemonde, Prince Golaud finds the fragile Mélisande weeping by a spring in the forest and marries her; she and his younger half-brother Pelléas fall in love, and Golaud in jealousy kills Pelléas. Mélisande dies after giving birth. Instead of arias, the singers follow the natural inflections of French speech, and the orchestra creates atmosphere through subtle colours, while the most intense moments are often almost silent. Maeterlinck, who had wanted his mistress to sing the title role, publicly hoped for the opera's failure. The premiere divided critics but it soon became a cult among young musicians. It is a key work of operatic modernism.

title: Madama Butterfly
creator: Giacomo Puccini
type: Opera, two acts (originally), revised in three acts
location: La Scala, Milan, 17 February 1904; revised version Teatro Grande, Brescia, 28 May 1904
description: Madama Butterfly is based on David Belasco's play, itself drawn from a short story by John Luther Long. The American naval lieutenant Pinkerton marries the fifteen-year-old geisha Cio-Cio-San in Nagasaki, a marriage he does not take seriously. She waits faithfully for years with their son, singing 'Un bel dì'; when he returns with an American wife to take the boy, she kills herself. Puccini studied Japanese melodies, which he wove into the score, together with a quotation from The Star-Spangled Banner. The premiere at La Scala was a fiasco; after revisions it succeeded in Brescia three months later. Its depiction of Japan and its exoticism have been reconsidered in recent decades, but it remains one of the most performed operas.

title: Salome
creator: Richard Strauss
location: Königliches Opernhaus, Dresden, 9 December 1905
description: Strauss set Hedwig Lachmann's German translation of Oscar Wilde's play Salome, itself scandalous. The princess Salome is fascinated by the prophet Jochanaan (John the Baptist), imprisoned by her stepfather Herod, who rejects her. Herod lusts after Salome and promises her anything if she dances for him; after the Dance of the Seven Veils she demands Jochanaan's head on a silver platter, and in a long final scene she kisses the dead lips, before Herod orders her killed. The dissonant, richly orchestrated score caused a sensation; the opera was banned in London and Vienna and withdrawn from the Metropolitan Opera after one performance in 1907. Its success enabled Strauss to build a villa in Garmisch.

title: La mer
creator: Claude Debussy
location: Concerts Lamoureux, Paris, 15 October 1905
description: Debussy wrote La mer mainly in Burgundy and Jersey, far from the sea, which he said he preferred to know through memory. Its three movements are From Dawn to Noon on the Sea, Play of the Waves and Dialogue of the Wind and the Sea. Rather than painting literal pictures, the music evokes the changing light, motion and power of the sea through constantly transforming motifs and orchestral textures. At his request, the cover of the first edition reproduced part of Hokusai's woodblock print The Great Wave off Kanagawa. The first performance was poorly received, partly due to the scandal of Debussy's divorce. It later became one of the most frequently performed orchestral works of the twentieth century.

title: The Firebird
creator: Igor Stravinsky
location: Palais Garnier, Paris, 25 June 1910, Ballets Russes, choreographed by Michel Fokine
description: Diaghilev commissioned The Firebird after Anatoly Lyadov failed to deliver the score. The story combines Russian folk tales: Prince Ivan captures the magical Firebird, who gives him a feather in exchange for her freedom; he later uses it to overcome the immortal sorcerer Kashchei and free thirteen princesses. Stravinsky, then twenty-eight, wrote a brilliant score in the style of his teacher Rimsky-Korsakov, using chromatic harmonies for the magic world and Russian folk melodies for the human characters. The premiere was a triumph. Stravinsky later made three concert suites, and the Infernal Dance of Kashchei, the Berceuse and the Finale became popular.

title: Das Lied von der Erde
creator: Gustav Mahler
type: Song-symphony for tenor, alto (or baritone) and orchestra
location: Munich, 20 November 1911, conducted by Bruno Walter (posthumous)
description: Mahler wrote The Song of the Earth in 1908–09, after the death of his daughter and the diagnosis of his heart disease. It sets six poems from Hans Bethge's Die chinesische Flöte, free German adaptations of Tang-dynasty Chinese poems, including several attributed to Li Bai. Mahler, reportedly superstitious about writing a ninth symphony after Beethoven, Schubert and Bruckner had died after theirs, did not number it. The songs alternate between tenor and alto, from the drinking song of the earth's misery to youth, beauty and the drunkard in spring. The final movement, Der Abschied (The Farewell), lasts about half an hour and ends with the word 'ewig' (forever) repeated over a sustained chord. It was premiered after Mahler's death by his assistant Bruno Walter.

title: Der Rosenkavalier
creator: Richard Strauss
location: Königliches Opernhaus, Dresden, 26 January 1911
description: Der Rosenkavalier (The Knight of the Rose), with a libretto by Hugo von Hofmannsthal, is set in Maria Theresa's Vienna. The Marschallin, a princess in her thirties, has a young lover, Octavian. Octavian is sent to present a silver rose to Sophie on behalf of the boorish Baron Ochs, but falls in love with her. The Marschallin, reflecting on time and age, gives him up, and the opera ends with a trio for three sopranos (Octavian is a trouser role) and a duet. Strauss filled the score with anachronistic waltzes and lush harmony, a deliberate turn from the modernism of Elektra. The premiere was such a success that special trains ran from Berlin to Dresden. It is one of the most beloved operas of the twentieth century.

title: Petrushka
creator: Igor Stravinsky
location: Théâtre du Châtelet, Paris, 13 June 1911, Ballets Russes, with Nijinsky as Petrushka
description: Petrushka began as a concert piece for piano and orchestra, which Diaghilev persuaded Stravinsky to turn into a ballet. With the designer Alexandre Benois, he set it at a Shrovetide fair in Saint Petersburg in the 1830s, where a magician brings three puppets to life: the sad Petrushka, the Ballerina and the brutal Moor. Petrushka, jealous of the Moor, is killed by him, and his ghost appears above the theatre. The 'Petrushka chord', combining C major and F-sharp major triads, symbolises the puppet's double nature. Stravinsky used street songs and folk tunes, and created layered textures of the fair's crowds. Vaslav Nijinsky danced the title role at the premiere, choreographed by Fokine.

title: Symphony No. 9
creator: Gustav Mahler
location: Vienna, 26 June 1912, Vienna Philharmonic conducted by Bruno Walter (posthumous)
description: Mahler wrote his Ninth Symphony in 1909–10 in his summer composing hut in Toblach, South Tyrol, and between his conducting seasons in New York. Like the Pathétique of Tchaikovsky, it ends with a slow movement. The first movement, with its hesitant rhythm, which some have linked to Mahler's irregular heartbeat, builds to catastrophic climaxes; the second is a grotesque series of Ländler; the third a savage Rondo-Burleske. The final Adagio fades away into near silence over its last pages, marked ersterbend (dying away). Alban Berg described the first movement as the most heavenly thing Mahler wrote. Bruno Walter conducted the premiere after Mahler's death.

title: Daphnis et Chloé
creator: Maurice Ravel
type: Ballet (choreographic symphony), one act in three parts
location: Théâtre du Châtelet, Paris, 8 June 1912, Ballets Russes, choreographed by Michel Fokine
description: Ravel wrote Daphnis et Chloé for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, based on the ancient Greek novel by Longus about the love of a shepherd and shepherdess on the island of Lesbos. Chloé is abducted by pirates, and the god Pan comes to her rescue. Ravel called it a choreographic symphony and built it from a few recurring themes. The orchestra is enormous and includes a wordless chorus. The ballet's premiere, with Vaslav Nijinsky and Tamara Karsavina, was overshadowed by Nijinsky's scandalous L'après-midi d'un faune in the same season. The music survives mainly in the two concert suites, especially the second, which opens with the sunrise, a radiant passage of murmuring strings and birdsong.

title: Pierrot lunaire
creator: Arnold Schoenberg
type: Melodrama for reciter and five players, Op. 21
location: Choralion-Saal, Berlin, 16 October 1912, with Albertine Zehme
description: The actress Albertine Zehme commissioned Pierrot lunaire, setting twenty-one poems by the Belgian Albert Giraud in Otto Erich Hartleben's German translation, about the commedia dell'arte clown Pierrot, intoxicated by moonlight, in visions of violence, religion and nostalgia. Schoenberg wrote it for a reciter and five players on eight instruments. The voice uses Sprechstimme, a half-spoken, half-sung delivery whose exact performance is still debated. The music is atonal, but within it Schoenberg uses old forms such as canons, a passacaglia and a fugue. Stravinsky, who attended a performance in 1912, called it the solar plexus of early twentieth-century music. Its instrumental combination, the Pierrot ensemble, became a standard for later composers.

title: The Rite of Spring (Le sacre du printemps)
creator: Igor Stravinsky
location: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris, 29 May 1913, Ballets Russes, choreographed by Vaslav Nijinsky
description: The Rite of Spring was conceived by Stravinsky and the painter and archaeologist Nicholas Roerich, who designed the sets and costumes, as a series of scenes of prehistoric Russian rituals celebrating the coming of spring, culminating in a young girl dancing herself to death. It opens with a high bassoon solo based on a Lithuanian folk melody and moves through violent, irregular rhythms, polytonal harmonies and hammering ostinatos. At the premiere, Nijinsky's choreography, with its turned-in feet and heavy stamping, and the music provoked an uproar in the audience, with shouting and fights that, according to some accounts, drowned out the orchestra; the extent of the riot has probably been exaggerated in later accounts. A year later, the concert performance in Paris was a triumph. It is considered one of the most influential works of the twentieth century.

title: Symphony No. 5 in E-flat major
creator: Jean Sibelius
location: Helsinki, 8 December 1915 (Sibelius's 50th birthday); final version 24 November 1919
description: Sibelius wrote his Fifth Symphony for celebrations of his fiftieth birthday in 1915 during the First World War, then revised it twice; the final version of 1919 has three movements instead of four. In April 1915 he wrote in his diary of seeing sixteen swans circling above him, one of the greatest experiences of his life. Their motion inspired the great theme of the finale, a swinging, bell-like idea in the horns, which he called the swan hymn. The first movement fuses a slow movement and a scherzo, accelerating continuously; the symphony ends with six widely spaced chords separated by silence. It is the most popular of his symphonies.

title: Rhapsody in Blue
creator: George Gershwin
type: Rhapsody for piano and jazz band
location: Aeolian Hall, New York, 12 February 1924, Paul Whiteman's orchestra with Gershwin as soloist
description: The bandleader Paul Whiteman announced a concert entitled An Experiment in Modern Music, and Gershwin found from a newspaper that he was writing a jazz concerto for it. He composed it in about three weeks, and Ferde Grofé orchestrated it for Whiteman's jazz band. It opens with a clarinet trill and a rising wail; according to legend the glissando was developed by Whiteman's clarinettist Ross Gorman during rehearsals. The work alternates piano solos, jazz-band episodes and a broad romantic melody. In the audience were Rachmaninoff, Stravinsky, Heifetz and Sousa. Later orchestrated for full symphony orchestra, it became a symbol of the Jazz Age and of New York.

title: Wozzeck
creator: Alban Berg
location: Berlin State Opera, 14 December 1925, conducted by Erich Kleiber
description: Berg saw Georg Büchner's fragmentary play Woyzeck in Vienna in 1914 and decided to set it. The soldier Wozzeck, abused by his Captain and used as a guinea pig by the Doctor, discovers that Marie, the mother of his child, is having an affair with a Drum Major. He stabs her by a pond and drowns trying to wash away the blood, while their son plays, unaware. Berg's experiences in the army during the First World War informed the work. Each of the fifteen scenes is based on a traditional musical form, such as a suite, a passacaglia or a sonata, though Berg did not want the audience to notice this. The music is largely atonal, with an orchestral interlude in D minor before the final scene. The premiere required 137 rehearsals. Wozzeck is one of the most important operas of the twentieth century.

title: Boléro
creator: Maurice Ravel
location: Paris Opéra, 22 November 1928, danced by Ida Rubinstein
description: The dancer Ida Rubinstein commissioned Boléro from Ravel for her company. Ravel described it as an experiment: a single melody in two parts, repeated eighteen times over an insistent snare-drum rhythm, with no development, only an orchestral crescendo, as each repetition is given to different instruments and combinations. In the last minutes the music modulates abruptly and collapses. Ravel was surprised by its popularity, and once said it contained no music. The original choreography by Bronislava Nijinska was set in a Spanish tavern. It became one of the most performed orchestral works of the twentieth century, and its copyright long earned huge royalties.

title: West End Blues
creator: Louis Armstrong
type: Jazz recording (Louis Armstrong and His Hot Five)
location: Recorded for Okeh Records, Chicago, 28 June 1928
description: West End Blues was written by King Oliver, Armstrong's mentor, and named after a resort on Lake Pontchartrain in New Orleans. Armstrong recorded it in Chicago in 1928 with his Hot Five, including the pianist Earl Hines. It opens with a dazzling unaccompanied trumpet cadenza, then moves through a slow blues with solos for trombone and clarinet, the latter in call and response with Armstrong's wordless scat singing, and a piano solo by Hines, before Armstrong returns with a long held high note and a descending phrase. The recording showed that jazz improvisation could reach the expressive and structural ambition of composed music. It was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1974.

title: Symphony, Op. 21
creator: Anton Webern
location: League of Composers, New York, 18 December 1929
description: Webern's Symphony is scored for a small ensemble of clarinet, bass clarinet, two horns, harp and strings, and lasts only about ten minutes. Its twelve-tone row is a palindrome: its second half is a reverse of the first. The first movement consists of double canons in mirror form, and the second is a theme with seven variations that is itself symmetrical around its centre. The notes are scattered between instruments in sparse points of sound, a style sometimes called pointillism. When performed in New York in 1929, it baffled the audience. After 1945, young composers such as Boulez and Stockhausen took it as a model for total serialism.

title: Symphony of Psalms
creator: Igor Stravinsky
location: Palais des Beaux-Arts, Brussels, 13 December 1930; Boston premiere 19 December 1930
description: The conductor Serge Koussevitzky commissioned this symphony for the fiftieth anniversary of the Boston Symphony Orchestra, but its premiere took place in Brussels a few days earlier. Stravinsky, who had returned to the Russian Orthodox Church in 1926, set Latin texts from the Psalms in the Vulgate translation. He omitted violins, violas and clarinets, giving prominence to woodwinds, brass, two pianos and a harp. The first movement is a prayer, the second a double fugue, and the third, the longest, ends with a slow 'Laudate Dominum' over a repeated figure in the bass, like bells. It is one of the masterpieces of Stravinsky's neoclassical period.

title: Mood Indigo
creator: Duke Ellington
type: Jazz composition (Duke Ellington and His Orchestra)
location: Recorded in New York, October 1930 (first released as Dreamy Blues)
description: Mood Indigo, credited to Ellington, Barney Bigard and Irving Mills, was first recorded in October 1930 under the title Dreamy Blues and became one of Ellington's first big hits. Its famous opening chorus places a muted trumpet, a muted trombone and a clarinet in its low register in an unusual voicing, the trombone playing at the top and the clarinet at the bottom; the overtones of the microphones of the time produced what Ellington called a 'mike tone'. Ellington later said he wrote it in fifteen minutes while waiting for dinner. It shows his talent for creating new sonorities from the particular sounds of his players. Lyrics were added later, and it became a jazz standard.

title: Violin Concerto, 'To the memory of an angel'
creator: Alban Berg
location: Palau de la Música Catalana, Barcelona, 19 April 1936, with Louis Krasner as soloist
description: The American violinist Louis Krasner commissioned a concerto from Berg, but he did not begin work until April 1935, when Manon Gropius, the eighteen-year-old daughter of Alma Mahler and the architect Walter Gropius, died of polio. Berg dedicated it to her memory. Its twelve-tone row is built from a chain of triads and ends with four rising whole-tone notes that coincide with the start of the Bach chorale Es ist genug (It is enough), which Berg quotes in its original harmonisation in the final movement. The concerto also includes a Carinthian folk song. Berg died before its premiere, so it became a requiem for him too.

title: Porgy and Bess
creator: George Gershwin
location: Colonial Theatre, Boston, 30 September 1935 (tryout); Alvin Theatre, New York, 10 October 1935
description: Porgy and Bess is based on DuBose Heyward's novel Porgy and the play by DuBose and Dorothy Heyward, with lyrics by DuBose Heyward and Ira Gershwin. Set in Catfish Row, a fictional African American tenement in Charleston, South Carolina, it tells of the disabled beggar Porgy, who tries to rescue Bess from her violent lover Crown and the drug dealer Sportin' Life. Gershwin called it a folk opera and insisted on an all-Black cast of classically trained singers. Its songs, including Summertime, I Got Plenty o' Nuttin' and It Ain't Necessarily So, mix jazz, blues, spirituals and operatic writing. The first Broadway run was a financial failure. Some African American critics criticised its stereotypes, and its reception is still debated, but the Metropolitan Opera staged it in 1985 and it is now part of the international repertory.

title: Peter and the Wolf
creator: Sergei Prokofiev
type: Symphonic fairy tale for narrator and orchestra, Op. 67
location: Moscow, 2 May 1936
description: Natalia Sats, director of the Central Children's Theatre in Moscow, commissioned Prokofiev to write a work introducing children to the instruments of the orchestra. He wrote both the text and music within a few weeks. A narrator tells the story of the young Peter, who, ignoring his grandfather's warnings, captures a wolf with the help of a bird, while the hunters arrive too late. Each character has an instrument and a theme: Peter the strings, the bird a flute, the duck an oboe, the cat a clarinet, the grandfather a bassoon, the wolf three horns and the hunters woodwind and timpani. It has been recorded with narrators ranging from Eleanor Roosevelt to David Bowie.

title: Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta
creator: Béla Bartók
location: Basel, 21 January 1937, Basel Chamber Orchestra conducted by Paul Sacher
description: Paul Sacher commissioned this work for the tenth anniversary of the Basel Chamber Orchestra. Bartók divided the strings into two groups placed on either side of the stage, with percussion, piano, harp and celesta in the middle. The first movement is a slow fugue that grows from a single chromatic subject and expands and contracts symmetrically, its climax placed close to the golden section, a proportion some analysts find throughout Bartók's music. The third movement, an eerie Adagio, is a classic example of his night music, with glissandi on timpani and shimmering celesta. Stanley Kubrick used it in The Shining (1980).

title: Symphony No. 5 in D minor
creator: Dmitri Shostakovich
location: Leningrad Philharmonic Hall, 21 November 1937, conducted by Yevgeny Mravinsky
description: Shostakovich wrote his Fifth Symphony in 1937, at the height of Stalin's Great Terror, a year after Pravda's attack on his opera Lady Macbeth. A newspaper article attributed to him called the work a Soviet artist's creative reply to just criticism, though he probably did not choose the phrase. At the premiere the audience gave an ovation of over half an hour, and many listeners wept during the slow movement. The finale ends in a long D major blaze, which can sound triumphal or, as the disputed memoir Testimony claims, a forced rejoicing, like being beaten with a stick and told to celebrate. The debate over its meaning continues. It remains Shostakovich's most popular symphony.

title: Romeo and Juliet
creator: Sergei Prokofiev
location: Mahen Theatre, Brno, 30 December 1938; Kirov Theatre, Leningrad, 11 January 1940
description: Prokofiev wrote Romeo and Juliet for the Kirov in Leningrad and then the Bolshoi in Moscow, but the theatres rejected it as undanceable, and an early version with a happy ending caused controversy. It was finally staged in Brno in Czechoslovakia in 1938, and in Leningrad in 1940, choreographed by Leonid Lavrovsky, with Galina Ulanova as Juliet. The score portrays the characters vividly, from the menacing Dance of the Knights of the Montagues and Capulets to the tender music of Juliet as a young girl and the tragic final scenes. The concert suites Prokofiev extracted helped it gain popularity. It is now one of the most performed full-length ballets.

title: Quartet for the End of Time (Quatuor pour la fin du temps)
creator: Olivier Messiaen
type: Chamber work for clarinet, violin, cello and piano
location: Stalag VIII-A prisoner-of-war camp, Görlitz, Silesia, 15 January 1941
description: Messiaen was captured as a soldier in 1940 and held at Stalag VIII-A at Görlitz, where he found among his fellow prisoners a clarinettist, a violinist and a cellist. He wrote the quartet for them and himself at the piano, and it was performed before an audience of prisoners and guards in January 1941, in the cold, on instruments in poor condition. Its eight movements are inspired by the angel of the Apocalypse in the Book of Revelation, who announces that there shall be time no longer. They include a solo for clarinet, Abyss of the Birds, an energetic dance of fury in unison, and two long, slow songs of praise to the eternity and immortality of Jesus, for cello and violin with piano. Messiaen's account of the premiere, including the number of listeners, has been questioned by historians. It is one of the most performed chamber works of the twentieth century.

title: Symphony No. 7 in C major, 'Leningrad'
creator: Dmitri Shostakovich
location: Kuybyshev (Samara), 5 March 1942; Leningrad, 9 August 1942, during the siege
description: Shostakovich began the Seventh Symphony in Leningrad in the summer of 1941, after the German invasion of the Soviet Union, and completed it after being evacuated to Kuybyshev. The first movement contains a long 'invasion' episode in which a banal march theme is repeated over a snare drum, building to a terrifying climax. The score was flown to the West on microfilm, and Toscanini conducted it in New York in 1942. On 9 August 1942 it was performed in besieged Leningrad by the surviving members of the radio orchestra, reinforced by soldiers, and broadcast by loudspeaker towards the German lines. Whether the invasion theme also refers to Stalin's repression has been debated. Later critics dismissed it as propaganda, but it has been regularly revived.

title: Black, Brown and Beige
creator: Duke Ellington
location: Carnegie Hall, New York, 23 January 1943
description: Ellington premiered Black, Brown and Beige at his first Carnegie Hall concert in 1943, a fundraiser for Russian war relief. Lasting about forty-five minutes, it was described as a tone parallel to the history of African Americans, from Africa and slavery (Black), through emancipation and the contributions of Black soldiers (Brown) to life in Harlem in the 1920s and 1930s (Beige). It includes the spiritual-like melody Come Sunday, played by the alto saxophonist Johnny Hodges. Some critics, both jazz and classical, received it coolly, and Ellington never again recorded it complete, preferring excerpts. It is now recognised as a landmark attempt to create extended composition in jazz.

title: Fanfare for the Common Man
creator: Aaron Copland
location: Cincinnati, 12 March 1943, Cincinnati Symphony Orchestra conducted by Eugene Goossens
description: In 1942 the conductor Eugene Goossens asked American composers to write fanfares to open concerts of the Cincinnati Symphony Orchestra as a contribution to the war effort. Copland's title was inspired by a speech by Vice President Henry Wallace proclaiming the century of the common man. Scored for brass and percussion, its slow, wide-spaced themes, interrupted by timpani and bass drum, create an impression of vastness. Goossens premiered it at income tax time, which Copland thought appropriate. He later reused it in the finale of his Third Symphony. It has been widely used at public events and covered by the rock group Emerson, Lake and Palmer.

title: Concerto for Orchestra
creator: Béla Bartók
location: Symphony Hall, Boston, 1 December 1944, Boston Symphony Orchestra conducted by Serge Koussevitzky
description: Bartók, ill and depressed in American exile, received a commission for an orchestral work from Serge Koussevitzky in 1943, which revived him. He explained that the title referred to the way single instruments or groups are treated in a concertante or soloistic manner. Its five movements move from darkness to life. The second, Game of Pairs, presents wind instruments in pairs at different intervals; the fourth, Interrupted Intermezzo, parodies a march theme from Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony, then widely broadcast; and the brilliant finale is based on folk dances. It became one of the most popular orchestral works of the twentieth century.

title: Appalachian Spring
creator: Aaron Copland
location: Library of Congress, Washington, D.C., 30 October 1944, Martha Graham Dance Company
description: Copland wrote this ballet for the dancer and choreographer Martha Graham, commissioned by the patron Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge. Its scenario concerns a young pioneer couple building a farmhouse in Pennsylvania in the early nineteenth century, with a revivalist preacher and a pioneer woman. The original score was for thirteen instruments; the orchestral suite of 1945 made it famous. Graham suggested the title, from a poem by Hart Crane, after the music was written. Its open, spacious harmonies and the variations on the Shaker song Simple Gifts became an image of American landscape and community. It won the Pulitzer Prize for Music in 1945.

title: Peter Grimes
creator: Benjamin Britten
type: Opera, prologue and three acts, Op. 33
location: Sadler's Wells Theatre, London, 7 June 1945
description: Britten read an article by E. M. Forster about the Suffolk poet George Crabbe while in California in 1941, and decided to write an opera on Crabbe's poem The Borough. The libretto, by Montagu Slater, portrays Peter Grimes, a rough, isolated fisherman suspected of having caused the death of his young apprentices, who is driven by the hostility of the townspeople to sail out to sea and sink his boat. The Four Sea Interludes evoke the North Sea coast in different moods. The opera, premiered a month after the end of the war in Europe, with Peter Pears in the title role, was a triumph and established Britten as a leading opera composer. Its theme of the outsider persecuted by the crowd has often been linked to his position as a gay man and pacifist.

title: Sonatas and Interludes
creator: John Cage
location: Carnegie Recital Hall, New York, 12 January 1949, Maro Ajemian
description: Cage invented the prepared piano in 1940 in Seattle, when he needed a percussion sound for a dance but had no room for percussion instruments. In Sonatas and Interludes, sixteen sonatas and four interludes, he prescribed precisely where to place screws, bolts, pieces of rubber and plastic between the strings of 45 notes, turning the piano into a delicate percussion orchestra that recalls the Balinese gamelan. Cage had become interested in Indian philosophy, and the cycle attempts to express the nine permanent emotions of Indian aesthetics. It is among his most performed works and won him a Guggenheim fellowship.

title: Turangalîla-Symphonie
creator: Olivier Messiaen
type: Symphony for piano, ondes Martenot and orchestra
location: Symphony Hall, Boston, 2 December 1949, Boston Symphony Orchestra conducted by Leonard Bernstein
description: Serge Koussevitzky commissioned Turangalîla for the Boston Symphony Orchestra, and the young Leonard Bernstein conducted the premiere. The title combines two Sanskrit words, which Messiaen explained as meaning love song, hymn to joy, time, movement, rhythm, life and death. It is the central work of a trilogy on the theme of Tristan and Isolde. Its ten movements use a huge orchestra with prominent piano, played at the premiere by Yvonne Loriod, and the ondes Martenot, an early electronic instrument with a sliding, eerie tone. Recurring themes include the heavy 'statue theme' and a tender 'love theme', and the rhythms are inspired by Indian talas. It is one of the most performed large orchestral works of the post-war era.

creator: John Cage
type: Piece in three movements for any instrument(s)
location: Maverick Concert Hall, Woodstock, New York, 29 August 1952, David Tudor (piano)
description: In 4′33″ the performer or performers are instructed not to play their instruments for the duration of the piece, divided into three movements. At the premiere the pianist David Tudor sat at the piano, closed the lid to mark the start of each movement and opened it at the end, while the audience heard the wind, rain on the roof and their own murmurs. Cage was inspired by Zen Buddhism, by Robert Rauschenberg's all-white paintings and by his visit to an anechoic chamber at Harvard, where he heard sounds of his own body and concluded that there is no such thing as silence. The piece is about listening to the sounds of the environment as music. It was mocked and celebrated in equal measure and is one of the most discussed works of the twentieth century.

title: Gesang der Jünglinge
creator: Karlheinz Stockhausen
location: WDR Cologne, broadcast concert, 30 May 1956
description: Stockhausen produced Gesang der Jünglinge (Song of the Youths) at the electronic music studio of West German Radio in Cologne. It is based on the Song of the Three Holy Children from the Book of Daniel, who praise God in the fiery furnace. Stockhausen recorded a boy singing the text and combined it with electronically generated sounds, from pure sine tones to noise, aiming for a continuum between vocal and electronic sound, with the words sometimes intelligible and sometimes broken into sounds. It was originally composed for five groups of loudspeakers surrounding the audience, an early experiment in spatial sound. It is regarded as one of the first masterpieces of electronic music.

title: String Quartet No. 8 in C minor
creator: Dmitri Shostakovich
location: Glinka Hall, Leningrad, 2 October 1960, Beethoven Quartet
description: Shostakovich wrote this quartet in three days in July 1960 while in Dresden, a city still in ruins from the Allied bombing of 1945, to work on a film score. Officially it is dedicated to the victims of fascism and war, but in a letter to his friend Isaak Glikman he wrote that he had dedicated it to his own memory. The five movements are played without pause, and nearly every one is based on his musical monogram, D-E flat-C-B (in German D-S-C-H), with quotations from his earlier works, a Jewish theme from his Piano Trio No. 2 and a revolutionary song. It came just after he had been pressured to join the Communist Party. It is his most often performed quartet.

title: Atmosphères
creator: György Ligeti
location: Donaueschingen Festival, 22 October 1961, SWF Symphony Orchestra conducted by Hans Rosbaud
description: Ligeti wrote Atmosphères for the Donaueschingen Festival of contemporary music, and its success made him one of the leading figures of the avant-garde. It opens with a huge chord containing all the notes of the chromatic scale over five octaves, played softly, and develops through dense clusters in which each instrumentalist plays a separate part. Changes of colour and texture take the place of melody and rhythm. Ligeti called the technique micropolyphony. Stanley Kubrick used it in 2001: A Space Odyssey, without the composer's consent, during the star gate sequence, which made it widely known.

title: War Requiem
creator: Benjamin Britten
location: St Michael's Cathedral, Coventry, 30 May 1962
description: Britten wrote the War Requiem for the consecration of the new Coventry Cathedral, built next to the ruins of the medieval cathedral destroyed by German bombing in 1940. He interwove the Latin requiem mass, sung by soprano, chorus and orchestra, with nine poems by Wilfred Owen, killed in the last week of the First World War, sung by tenor and baritone with a chamber orchestra, and a boys' choir with organ placed in the distance. He intended the three soloists to be from Britain, Germany and the Soviet Union, though the Soviet soprano Galina Vishnevskaya was not allowed to travel for the premiere. The work ends with Owen's Strange Meeting, in which two dead soldiers from opposing sides meet. The Decca recording of 1963 sold hundreds of thousands of copies.

title: In C
creator: Terry Riley
type: Work for any number of performers
location: San Francisco Tape Music Center, 4 November 1964
description: In C consists of a single page of 53 short musical phrases. Any number of performers, on any instruments, play through them in order, each deciding how many times to repeat each phrase before moving on, while a steady pulse on the note C, played on piano or mallet instruments, keeps the ensemble together. The result is a constantly shifting web of patterns, different in each performance, usually lasting between forty-five and ninety minutes. The idea of the pulse was suggested by Steve Reich, who played at the premiere. The 1968 recording on Columbia Records brought the work to a wide audience. It is often considered the first major minimalist composition.

title: Lux Aeterna
creator: György Ligeti
location: Stuttgart, 2 November 1966, Schola Cantorum Stuttgart conducted by Clytus Gottwald
description: Ligeti set the text of the communion from the Latin requiem mass, Lux aeterna luceat eis, Domine (May eternal light shine upon them, Lord), for sixteen solo voices. Each voice moves in strict canon at slightly different rhythms, so the individual lines blur into a slowly changing cloud of sound in which the words dissolve. The music moves from high women's voices down to low basses and back, giving the impression of light. Like Atmosphères, it was used in 2001: A Space Odyssey, in the scene on the Moon. It is one of the best-known choral works of the late twentieth century.

title: Music for 18 Musicians
creator: Steve Reich
location: The Town Hall, New York, 24 April 1976, Steve Reich and Musicians
description: Reich wrote Music for 18 Musicians for his own ensemble, which consists of violin, cello, two clarinets doubling bass clarinet, four women's voices, four pianos, three marimbas, two xylophones and a metallophone. The work begins and ends with a cycle of eleven chords, and each chord becomes the basis of a short section, lasting about five minutes. There is no conductor: the metallophone gives cues for changes, as in a Balinese gamelan or West African drumming, and the length of some passages depends on the breath of the singers and clarinettists. The 1978 ECM recording sold more than 100,000 copies, which was unusual for new music. It is often considered Reich's masterpiece and one of the defining works of minimalism.

title: Einstein on the Beach
creator: Philip Glass
location: Festival d'Avignon, 25 July 1976; Metropolitan Opera House, New York, November 1976
description: Glass and the director Robert Wilson created Einstein on the Beach, a work without a conventional plot about the figure of Albert Einstein, organised around images such as a train, a trial and a spaceship, connected by short interludes called knee plays. The texts include numbers, solfège syllables and spoken texts by Christopher Knowles, Lucinda Childs and Samuel M. Johnson. The music, for the amplified Philip Glass Ensemble, chorus and solo violin, is built on repeated patterns, with additive rhythmic processes. It lasts around five hours without an interval, and the audience is free to come and go. The two sold-out performances at the Metropolitan Opera in 1976 left Glass in debt. It is regarded as a landmark of contemporary opera.

title: Tabula rasa
creator: Arvo Pärt
type: Double concerto for two violins, string orchestra and prepared piano
location: Tallinn, 30 September 1977, Gidon Kremer and Tatiana Grindenko
description: Tabula rasa was written for the violinists Gidon Kremer and Tatiana Grindenko and the conductor Eri Klas. It is in two movements: Ludus (Game), in which the soloists and orchestra repeat and expand phrases separated by silences, building to a climax, and Silentium, a slow, multi-layered canon in which the voices move at different speeds and gradually sink into silence. It uses the tintinnabuli technique that Pärt had developed the year before, in which one voice outlines a triad while another moves stepwise. Its 1984 recording on the ECM label introduced Pärt to Western audiences.

title: Spiegel im Spiegel
creator: Arvo Pärt
type: Duo for violin (or cello) and piano
location: Written for the violinist Vladimir Spivakov, 1978
description: Spiegel im Spiegel (Mirror in the Mirror) was one of Pärt's last works written before he left the Soviet Union. A violin plays slow, simple scale phrases that grow by one note each time, moving alternately up and down from the note A, over a piano accompaniment of rising triads in F major, with deep bass notes and high bell-like notes. The title refers to the infinity of images produced by parallel mirrors. Its calm simplicity has made it one of Pärt's most popular works, used in many films and dance pieces.
